title: Governing the post-consolidation mega-city: legal frameworks for digital transformation in Da Nang, Vietnam
summary: This study evaluates the legal framework for digital transformation in local governance in Da Nang, Vietnam, following its administrative consolidation. Through the analysis of secondary documents and in-depth interviews across five stakeholder groups, the paper asserts that despite a successful transition toward an "enabling development" paradigm-driving the digital economy to account for 24% of the GRDP (in 2024)-the system remains constrained by five core bottlenecks. These include vertical regulatory misalignment, data siloing, rigid public finance, the absence of digital personnel standards, and the digital divide across regions. The study proposes a comprehensive matrix of solutions toward 2035, emphasizing regulatory sandboxes and public service co-production, while concurrently integrating green transformational leadership into grassroots administrative capacities. This research provides empirical implications for refining digital transformation laws within polycentric urban governance in emerging economies undergoing institutional transitions.

title: Environmental, Social & Governance Performance Research Report Fiscal Year 2023 — Comprehensive ESG Analysis with 26 Data Visualizations
summary: This research paper provides a comprehensive quantitative and qualitative assessment of Citigroup Inc. Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance for fiscal year 2023. Drawing upon Citigroup official ESG Report, TCFD disclosure, and Climate Report, as well as third-party ratings from MSCI, Sustainalytics, and Refinitiv, this paper synthesizes 26 original data visualizations to present a rigorous analysis of Citi sustainability trajectory. Key findings include: cumulative sustainable finance activity of $441 billion against a $1 trillion 2030 target; a 49% reduction in Scope 2 GHG emissions relative to the 2010 baseline, exceeding the 45% interim target; achievement of 100% renewable electricity sourcing for the fourth consecutive year; an MSCI ESG rating of A and a Refinitiv score of 85/100; and advancement of net-zero interim emission targets across six high-carbon sectors. Social performance highlights include 40.6% women in leadership (AVP to MD level), adjusted pay equity ratios of 99 cents per dollar for women and U.S. minority employees, and $6.5 billion in affordable housing loan originations. The paper concludes with a detailed ESG metrics framework, benchmarks against global banking peers, and strategic observations regarding transition risk, governance quality, and the credibility of Citi net-zero pathway.

title: Digital Technology Adoption and Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Risk Management: Evidence from West Java, Indonesia
summary: Background: The increasing complexity of pharmaceutical supply chains, along with regulatory pressure and operational disruptions, has created an urgent need for effective supply chain risk management. Digital technology adoption is considered essential for improving operational resilience and continuity. Objective: The purpose of this research is to analyses the effect of digital technology adoption on supply chain risk management performance in pharmaceutical companies in West Java Province, Indonesia. Methods: This study used a quantitative approach with Partial Least Squares–Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected through structured questionnaires distributed to managers in pharmaceutical manufacturing, distribution, and logistics companies. A total of 100 valid responses were analyzed to evaluate the relationships among technological infrastructure, digital system utilization, and supply chain risk management dimensions. Results: The findings show that technological infrastructure significantly influences digital system utilization (β = 0.712; p < 0.001), while digital system utilization positively affects supply chain risk management performance (β = 0.684; p < 0.001). The model produced an R² value of 0.63, indicating substantial explanatory power. In addition, digital technology adoption improved operational efficiency, delivery reliability, and supply chain resilience. Conclusion: This research confirms that digital technology adoption plays a significant role in strengthening supply chain risk management and supporting sustainable operational performance in the pharmaceutical industry.

title: Assessing the Economic Impact of Safety Investments on Supply Chain Performance in Large Construction Projects: A Case Study of the Third Ring Road Project in Tripoli, Libya
summary: The construction industry is highly hazardous, where accidents cause human and financial losses and disrupt supply chains. This study investigates the economic impact of safety investments on supply chain performance, using the Third Ring Road Project in Tripoli, Libya, as a case study. A quantitative survey of 49 professionals was analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics (Pearson correlation). Findings show high agreement on safety's importance (mean=4.15). Critically, accident reduction is the strongest driver of supply chain resilience (r=0.792, p<0.001), and safety investment significantly impacts economic performance (r=0.422, p=0.003). However, financial expenditure alone does not guarantee safety gains, as effectiveness depends on organizational culture and training. This study provides empirical evidence from Libya, offering practical guidance for integrating safety into strategic project management to enhance sustainability.

title: The Economics of Agri-Food Supply Chain Resilience: Pandemics, Climate Shocks and Global Disruptions
summary: Agri-food supply chain resilience has become a central economic concern as disease outbreaks, climatic extremes, trade restrictions and geopolitical disruptions expose interdependencies between production, processing, logistics, markets and household food access. Yet operational continuity alone is an incomplete measure of resilience: firms may recover output while consumers face unaffordable diets, workers lose earnings and costly buffers transfer risks between regions or supply-chain tiers. This critical narrative review examines how shocks propagate through agri-food systems, why decentralised incentives may diverge from social welfare, and which private and public responses are supported by credible evidence. Peer-reviewed empirical studies, theoretical analyses, simulations and substantive reviews published from 2004 to 4 September 2026 were assessed through targeted scholarly discovery, bibliographic verification and thematic appraisal, with earlier conceptual antecedents considered where necessary. The synthesis distinguishes covariate from localised shocks, physical scarcity from purchasing-power failures, and short-term recovery from economically and environmentally sustainable adaptation. Pandemic evidence indicates heterogeneous disruptions: substantial losses for particular workers, farmers and perishable-product channels coexisted with adaptive capacity in other markets. Climate research supports material agricultural supply risks, although uncertainty remains about cross-sector transmission and simultaneous harvest failures. Trade and conflict studies indicate that diversification can buffer geographically specific losses but may propagate correlated shortages and policy-induced price instability. Crucially, recent economic modelling shows that private investment in risk reduction need not always fall below the social optimum; market power and the interdependence of protective investments can also produce overinvestment. The review proposes a welfare-centred appraisal of resilience that incorporates consumer access, distributional incidence, risk covariance, fiscal costs and long-run adaptation rather than equating resilience with inventory, localisation or digitisation. Evidence gaps concern comparable causal estimates, systemic risk spillovers, low-income consumers, and prospective evaluations of combined interventions. Context-specific portfolios of risk reduction, trade openness, social protection and adaptive infrastructure appear more defensible than universal prescriptions.

title: The Structure and Evolution of China’s Green Finance Policy Instruments
summary: China’s green finance policy system consists of many separate measures, and most studies examine them one at a time. This paper describes the system as a whole. It asks which instruments the system contains and how their relative weight changed between the 2016 Guiding Opinions on Building a Green Financial System and 2025. The instruments are grouped into five categories: green credit, green bonds, green insurance, green funds and carbon finance. The description rests on three public sources: green loan statistics from the People’s Bank of China, green bond issuance data from the Climate Bonds Initiative, and the text of the policy documents. Green loans grew faster than total loans over the period, and their share of total loans rose from 6.7% at end-2020 to 16.2% at end-2025. Green bond issuance peaked in 2022 within the period covered and was about 18% lower in 2024 than in 2023. Both patterns need to be read with care, because the green loan statistics were redefined in 2025 and the bond figures come from report editions with different database cut-off dates. Read together with the policy documents, the evidence suggests that direct financial support has been joined by project standards, institutional assessment and risk management requirements. Government direction, market development and risk control are used here as three organising ideas for interpreting that combination. The paper describes how the system is built and how it has changed; it does not estimate the effect of any single policy.

title: How does collaboration shape supply chain resilience? Evidence from climate-exposed agri-food systems
summary: Purpose This study aims to investigate how supply chain resilience (SCR) emerges in agri-food supply chains under persistent climate stress. It examines the effects of specific supply chain collaboration mechanisms on SCR and evaluates whether entrepreneurial orientation (EO) serves as a behavioural enhancement pathway linking collaboration mechanisms to SCR. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in complex adaptive systems theory, the study adopts a chain-level perspective of resilience. Data were collected from 205 actors across multiple tiers of the Vietnamese smallholder coffee supply chain. Structural equation modelling was used to assess the direct effects of collaboration mechanisms on SCR and the mediating role of EO. Findings Operational collaboration mechanisms, namely information sharing, incentive alignment, decision synchronisation, communication and resource sharing, were positively associated with SCR. EO also had a positive effect on SCR and partially mediated the relationships between selected mechanisms (information sharing, incentive alignment and resource sharing) and SCR. The findings indicated that collaboration enhanced resilience through both operational coordination and behavioural adaptation pathways, while strategic alignment mechanisms showed delayed effects. Research limitations/implications The study is based on cross-sectional, perceptual data from a single commodity and regional context, which may limit generalisability. Future research should adopt longitudinal designs and examine diverse supply chain settings to further validate system-level and behavioural mechanisms of resilience. Practical implications Managers and policymakers should prioritise collaboration practices that strengthen information flows, align incentives and enable resource sharing. In parallel, fostering entrepreneurial behaviours among supply chain actors can enhance adaptive responses to climate-related disruptions. Originality/value This study contributes to SCR literature by unpacking collaboration into distinct mechanisms and identifying EO as a behavioural micro-foundation through which resilience emerges at the chain level in fragmented and decentralised supply chains.

title: Impacts of ESG disclosure intensity on trade credit: international evidence
summary: This study examines the relationship between ESG disclosure intensity and trade credit using firm-level data from 72 countries over the period 2009–2023. The empirical evidence reveals a U-shaped relationship between ESG disclosure intensity and trade credit. ESG disclosure intensity initially has a negative association with trade credit, but as disclosure intensity increases, its effect becomes more positive for both trade credit received from suppliers and trade credit granted to customers. These findings remain robust across alternative specifications and institutional settings. Among the ESG pillars, environmental and governance disclosures exhibit more pronounced and consistent effects than social disclosures. Overall, this study extends the literature on the nonlinear relationship between ESG disclosure intensity and trade credit and provides a more comprehensive understanding of the implications of ESG disclosure for firms’ trade credit management.

title: When resilience erodes itself: double machine learning evidence on extreme precipitation and supply chain resilience in the textile value chain
summary: We examine a capability paradox: extreme precipitation heightens the need for supply chain resilience (SCR) while depleting the resources required to sustain it. Using Chinese A-share firms in the textile value chain (2010–2024), we construct a five-dimensional SCR index and measure extreme precipitation using daily meteorological observations and city-specific percentile thresholds. Partially linear double machine learning, implemented with random forests, cross-fitting, and orthogonalization, indicates that extreme precipitation significantly weakens SCR. Mechanism tests reveal higher operating cost and selling expense ratios, more severe financing constraints, and increased debt financing costs. Cash holdings, sponge city construction, and political connections attenuate the adverse effect, while extreme precipitation also inhibits value chain upgrading. Results remain robust to alternative samples, model specifications, learning algorithms, resilience measures, and permutation-based placebo tests. The findings inform differentiated climate risk management by textile firms and government policies for climate adaptation.

title: The Role of Digital Transformation as A Mechanism to Attract Foreign Direct Investments in The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia: in the light of Vision 2030
summary: The research aimed to study the relationship between digital economy indicators (network readiness index, Internet service subscription rate index out of the total population, fixed and mobile phone subscriptions, broadband service subscriptions) as independent variables and the business environment and foreign direct investment index as dependent variables during the time period (2006). – 2023) with the application of the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) method and Robust regression in order to avoid the problem of Heteroskedasticity. The study found that there is only a positive and significant relationship between the network readiness index and foreign direct investment, while the index of the percentage of Internet service subscriptions out of the total population and broadband service subscriptions. The results showed the opposite of our expectations, which is negative and significant on foreign direct investment. In addition to this, the indicator of the percentage of Internet service subscriptions out of the total population, mobile phone subscriptions, and broadband service subscriptions have a positive statistical significance on the business environment index.

title: The Impact of Open Government Data on Green Innovation: The Mediating Roles of Environmental Governance and Human Capital in Chinese Prefecture-Level Cities
summary: Open government data (OGD) is a critical strategic measure for governments to unlock the value of data as a factor of production and a key approach to promoting high-quality economic development in the digital era. However, existing research has not sufficiently explored the specific mechanisms and contextual conditions under which OGD influences regional green innovation, creating a significant research gap. This paper aims to fill this gap by utilizing the introduction of OGD platforms by local governments in China as a quasi-natural experiment. Employing panel data from Chinese prefecture-level cities between 2007 and 2022, we investigate the impact of OGD on regional green innovation. The findings reveal that OGD significantly enhances regional green innovation, a conclusion that remains robust across a series of robustness checks. Mechanism analysis further indicates that OGD empowers regional green innovation partly through strengthening government environmental governance and augmenting advanced human capital support. Each of the two channels accounts for about 11% of the total effect. Heterogeneity analysis yields several clear findings: the promoting effect of OGD is more pronounced in eastern cities, higher-tier cities, cities with a greater focus on environmental protection, cities with higher levels of public environmental concern, and cities with stronger support for digital economy policies. Theoretically, this study contributes to the literature by elucidating the ‘black box’ of how OGD influences green innovation and identifying important boundary conditions. Practically, the findings provide empirical insights for policymakers seeking to maximize the empowering role of data factors in fostering regional green technological innovation.

title: Determinan manajemen laba: Arus kas operasi, profitabilitas, dan umur perusahaan pada perusahaan makanan dan minuman di Bursa Efek Indonesia
summary: Earnings management reduces the reliability of earnings information, yet evidence on its determinants remains inconsistent across settings and periods. Drawing on signaling theory and the bonus plan hypothesis, this study examines the effects of operating cash flow, profitability, and firm age on earnings management in food and beverage companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during 2022–2024. A quantitative associative design was applied to 58 firms selected through purposive sampling, yielding 174 firm-year observations, of which 149 remained after outlier screening. Earnings management was measured by signed discretionary accruals from the Modified Jones Model, and the data were analyzed with multiple linear regression after classical assumption testing. Operating cash flow is negatively and significantly associated with discretionary accruals, profitability is positively and significantly associated with them, and firm age is not significantly associated. Firms with stronger operating cash flow report accruals that raise income less, whereas more profitable firms report accruals that raise income more or lower it less. Because average discretionary accruals are negative, the results indicate the direction, not the magnitude, of accrual management. Investors and regulators should assess profit levels together with cash flow quality.

title: Copy, paste, and obfuscate? Readability and standardisation in integrated reporting
summary: Purpose This study examines how readability and textual similarity evolve and interact in integrated reports, investigating whether narrative accessibility and textual standardisation are distinct characteristics or interconnected features of institutionalised reporting practices. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal panel of 1,393 firm-year observations from South African listed companies over 2015–2024 is analysed. Readability is measured using Flesch Reading Ease, and textual similarity using cosine similarity between consecutive reports. Fixed-effects panel regressions are supplemented by governance-excluded similarity measures, first-difference models, persistence analysis and an alternative readability measure. Findings Readability declines over time, while textual similarity remains high, with no consistent upward trend. Textual similarity is positively associated with readability, indicating that narrative continuity can coexist with greater accessibility. However, this association becomes insignificant when governance-related disclosures are excluded, suggesting that it is concentrated within a highly institutionalised disclosure domain characterised by recurring reporting requirements and stable narrative structures. Additional analyses confirm the persistence of textual similarity and robustness of the main findings. Originality/value This study extends research that has largely examined readability and textual similarity separately by demonstrating that these characteristics are interrelated and that their association depends on the disclosure domain. Greater readability can coexist with substantial textual standardisation, complicating the interpretation of this as an unambiguous indicator of disclosure quality or transparency. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing narrative accessibility, textual standardisation and substantive informativeness when evaluating corporate disclosure.

title: The Impact of the Digital Economy on the High-Quality Development of Foreign Trade: Evidence from City-Level Panel Data in Anhui Province
summary: The digital economy is reshaping global trade and creating new opportunities for the high-quality development of foreign trade.Taking the prefecture-level cities of Anhui Province during 2010–2023 as the empirical sample,this paper constructs a composite index of digital economy development along four dimensions—digital infrastructure,digital industrialisation,the digitalisation of industry,and digital talent—and an index of the high-quality development of foreign trade covering foreign trade volume,foreign trade structure and foreign trade competitiveness, both measured using the entropy weight method.A two-way fixed effects model is estimated to examine the effect of the digital economy on the high-quality development of foreign trade in Anhui.The results show that the digital economy exerts a significantly positive promoting effect on the high-quality development of foreign trade in the province,and that this effect displays pronounced regional and temporal heterogeneity. The findings carry practical implications for how Chinese provinces can seize the opportunities of the digital era to advance the high-quality development of foreign trade.

title: Private sustainability engagement in an emerging economy
summary: Purpose This study critically examines how private sustainability engagement functions as a form of dialogic accountability when Nordic institutional investors interact with publicly listed companies in a state-dominated emerging economy, challenging the implicit universalism of consensus-seeking engagement models. Design/methodology/approach The study employs qualitative content analysis of Nordic investor engagement reports documenting extended interactions with Egyptian financial and telecommunication companies. Legitimacy theory, neo-institutional theory and dialogic accountability provide an integrated lens for examining information exchange and corporate answerability. Findings Private engagements centre on political connections and human rights risks, with documented response patterns consistent with a prioritisation of political licence to operate over substantive answerability to international investors. The documented engagements record evidential burdens preventing independent verification. The response patterns across both cases constitute dialogic deadlock – a structural ceiling where genuine accountability exchange is foreclosed. Originality/value Empirically, the study provides an in-depth qualitative content analysis of investor-side engagement reports, documenting the sustainability information Nordic investors seek in two Egyptian private engagements and the patterns of corporate response. Theoretically, it proposes political licence and audience primacy as concepts for interpreting the documented exchanges and specifies the contextual conditions under which audience hierarchy may shift toward audience primacy. Conceptually, it theorises dialogic deadlock as a structural outcome arising where legitimacy incentives prove insufficient and the preconditions for genuine dialogic accountability are constitutively absent.

title: Digital Transformation and Sustainable Development of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in South East, Nigeria
summary: This study examined the effect of digital transformation on the sustainable development of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in South East Nigeria, focusing on digital business process integration and economic sustainability, as well as digital infrastructure adoption and social sustainability. The study was motivated by the increasing importance of digital technologies driven by the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) and the need for SMEs to achieve long-term sustainability in business operations amidst the challenges facing SMEs in achieving sustainable development in emerging economies. The study was anchored on Resource-Based View (RBV) Theory and adopted a survey research design. The population comprised of 10,016 employees of selected registered SMEs, based on their involvement in business activities that require the use of digital technologies and their abilities to integrate and adapt these digital technologies in key business operations and processes. They consisted of 1,895 small enterprises and 8,121 medium enterprises across Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu and Imo States. Using the Krejcie and Morgan (1970) sample size table, 370 respondents were selected, while 364 valid responses were used for the analysis. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression at 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that digital business process integration had a positive and statistically significant effect on the economic sustainability of SMEs (R = .790, R² = .625, F(1, 362) = 602.675, β = .790, p = .001). The study also established that digital infrastructure adoption had a positive and statistically significant effect on the social sustainability of SMEs (R = .739, R² = .546, F(1, 362) = 434.455, β = .739, p = .001). The study concluded that digital business process integration and digital infrastructure adoption were important factors in promoting economic and social sustainability of SMEs in South East Nigeria. It recommended that SME owners and managers should adopt and integrate digital technologies across key business operations and that government agencies and telecommunications providers should promote access to reliable and affordable digital infrastructure to strengthen business operations, stakeholder participation and social inclusion and sustainability.

title: Corporate Social Responsibility (Csr) Reporting: Challenges and Opportunities for Small and Medium Enterprise's
summary: This study investigates the problems and opportunities in Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) reporting, concentrating on fragmented reporting standards, green-washing concerns, and resource restrictions facing firms, particularly Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs). This research employs an exploratory methodology using secondary data from academic journals, industry reports, and media sources to examine how standardisation challenges and operational bottlenecks erode stakeholder trust and diminish reporting efficacy. The results indicate that the lack of standardised frameworks (GRI, SASB, and TCFD) leads to issues in comparability, while substantial implementation costs and insufficient third-party certification methods exacerbate the risks of green-washing, as illustrated by incidents like Volkswagen's "Dieselgate" affair. Utilising Stakeholder Theory (Freeman, 1984) and Legitimacy Theory (Dowling & Pfeffer, 1975), the study illustrates that CSR reporting has transitioned from voluntary generosity to a strategic necessity, but structural obstacles remain. Opportunities arise from technical advances such as artificial intelligence and blockchain, standardised worldwide practices, and improved stakeholder participation. The study concluded that CSR reporting is no longer optional but crucial for creating trust, guaranteeing resilience, and securing competitive advantage. Recommendations include campaigning for consolidated reporting frameworks, utilising digital tools for cost-effective data management, and fostering multi-stakeholder engagement to turn CSR reporting from compliance burden into strategic value creation catalyst. Keywords: CSR reporting, Stakeholder theory, Green-washing, Sustainability, ESG frameworks, corporate accountability.

title: Pengaruh Herding Behavior dan Risk Aversion terhadap Partisipasi Investor Muda di Reksa Dana dengan Peran Fintech sebagai Mediator
summary: This study examines the effect of herding behavior and risk aversion on young investors' participation in mutual funds, with fintech as a mediating variable. A quantitative survey was conducted using a questionnaire distributed to 130 young investors aged 30 years or younger who had invested in mutual funds through fintech applications, selected by purposive sampling. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The results show that herding behavior has no significant direct effect on young investors' participation, whereas risk aversion has a positive and significant direct effect. Fintech positively and significantly affects participation and is positively influenced by herding behavior and risk aversion. Fintech fully mediates the effect of herding behavior on participation and partially mediates the effect of risk aversion. These findings indicate that fintech is a mechanism that channels the behavioral tendencies of young investors into actual participation in mutual fund investment.

title: PRE-ASSESSMENT OF FINANCIAL AUDIT DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN RA
summary: The rapid development of digital technologies and the introduction of new tools for processing financial information are significantly changing the methods and principles of organizing financial audits. The use of artificial intelligence, big data analysis, automation of robotic processes and cloud technologies creates new opportunities for increasing the efficiency of audit processes, assessing the reliability of financial information and timely identifying risks. At the same time, digital transformation poses a number of methodological, technological, organizational and professional issues, the solution of which is an important prerequisite for ensuring the quality, independence and credibility of the audit. The article substantiates the need for digital transformation of financial audit and presents the prerequisites for its effective implementation․

title: Corporate Artificial Intelligence and Green Innovation Efficiency: The Roles of Environmental Disclosure, R&D Human Capital and Government Subsidies
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely promoted as a tool for corporate green transformation, but whether it helps firms convert research and development (R&D) resources into green technologies more efficiently remains unclear. Drawing on the resource-based view and information-asymmetry theory, this study examines whether corporate AI is associated with green innovation efficiency (GEff), whether environmental information disclosure quality (Eidq) transmits this association, and whether government subsidies condition it. Using 28,219 firm-year observations of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2024, we measure AI with a text-based index from annual reports and estimate two-way fixed-effects models, complemented by leave-one-out instrumental variables, dynamic specifications, alternative measures including AI patents and bootstrap mediation tests. AI is positively and robustly associated with GEff, an association driven mainly by green invention patents, whereas past GEff does not predict future AI. Eidq and R&D human capital provide significant but modest partial mediating channels, and the AI–GEff association is stronger at higher subsidy levels, particularly for non-innovation subsidies. Formal tests reveal no significant differences across regions, pollution intensity, technology status, life-cycle stages, industries or ownership. The findings suggest that combining AI deployment with credible environmental disclosure and subsidies for AI adoption can support more efficient green innovation.

title: Technology dividend or governance black box? Digital transformation and ESG performance in Chinese energy firms
summary: Using 610 firm-year observations on 122 Chinese listed energy firms over 2020–2024, this paper examines the relationship between digital transformation and ESG performance, the mediating role of internal control quality and the moderating role of government subsidies. Digital transformation is positively associated with ESG performance in the controlled specification (coefficient 0.138, t = 2.32). Internal control quality carries a significant indirect effect of 0.035 (95% CI [0.008, 0.063]), while the direct effect becomes insignificant. Government subsidies strengthen the association (interaction coefficient 0.0452, t = 2.34). Industry analysis shows a stronger association in gas utilities than in power generation. The estimate becomes insignificant with firm fixed effects, and several alternative specifications are also insignificant; the findings therefore support a conditional association rather than a causal effect. The results highlight governance upgrading and the scale of public support as relevant considerations in energy-sector digitalisation.

title: Can agricultural green development policies improve the carbon performance of enterprises? Empirical evidence from listed agricultural enterprises in China
summary: Introduction Carbon management in agricultural enterprises is deeply embedded in the agricultural industrial ecosystem. The policy of green development in agriculture provides a key path to solve the predicament of carbon reduction in agriculture. Methods This paper, based on the microdata of 245 listed agricultural enterprises in China from 2011 to 2024, uses a dual machine learning model to investigate the impact of agricultural green development policies on the carbon performance (CP) of agricultural enterprises and its mechanism of action. Results The research findings are as follows: First, the green development policy for agriculture has significantly enhanced the CP of agricultural enterprises. Second, mechanism tests have shown that promoting green technological innovation, alleviating financing constraints, and increasing external media attention are the three core paths for agricultural green development policies to enhance the CP of agricultural enterprises. Thirdly, heterogeneity analysis indicates that this policy has a more significant effect on enhancing CP for agricultural enterprises located in the second batch of pilot zones, regions with strong environmental regulations, and those with lower digitalization levels. Fourth, an expansive analysis reveals that there is a significant synergy between the agricultural green development policy and the green finance reform and innovation pilot zone policy in enhancing the CP of agricultural enterprises, and the implementation effect of the compound policy is superior to that of a single policy. Discussion This article expands the research on the environmental effects of agricultural green development policies from the perspective of micro enterprises, providing empirical evidence and policy inspirations for optimizing the policy system of agricultural green development, strengthening policy coordination, and promoting the green and low-carbon transformation of agricultural enterprises.

title: Distribution of ESG Practices Among the Luse Sub-Industries Based on Morgan Stanley Capital International ESG Industry Materiality Map
summary: This paper assesses the distribution of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practices among the Lusaka Securities Exchange (LuSE) sub-industries, using the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) ESG Industry Materiality Map. The paper employs a descriptive quantitative research design and uses secondary data from annual audited reports, sustainability reports, and related corporate disclosures from 2019-2023, using a modified MSCI ESG industry materiality map and an industry-adjusted ESG scoring framework alongside a purposive sample of 12 firms with 60 firm-year observations. The findings show a generally high level of ESG adoption, with a mean ESG score of 6.52 for LUSE-listed firms but with a significant variation across the sub-industries. Governance emerged as the top-performing dimension, with social and environmental performance ranking second and third, respectively. We found that ESG outcomes reflected industry-specific sustainability risks in line with the MSCI ESG industry materiality map. The highest overall ESG scores were achieved by industrial conglomerates, independent power producers and energy traders, and forest products. Comparative average results were observed for the diversified real estate activities and reinsurance sub-industries. The highest score in environmental performance was Independent Power Producers & Energy Traders, in social was Diversified Financial Services, and in governance was Industrial Conglomerates. The findings indicate that there are significant differences in environmental, social, and governance distributions among LUSE sub-industries, suggesting that ESG practices are unevenly distributed among the LUSE sub-industries. The paper adds to the emerging market ESG literature and provides practical findings for policymakers, regulators, investors, and corporate managers who aim to enhance ESG integration, sustainability reporting, and long-term value creation within Zambia’s capital market

title: Bridging International Financial Reporting Standards and Emerging Market Realities: A Practical Framework for Accounting Education and Implementation
summary: The global adoption of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) aims to provide highquality, transparent, and comparable financial information across capital markets. However, inemerging markets, practitioners and students frequently encounter significant friction whentranslating abstract accounting standards into real-world commercial workflows.This paper presents an applied instructional and implementation framework designed to bridgethe gap between theoretical standards specifically IAS 1 (Presentation of Financial Statements),IAS 7 (Statement of Cash Flows), and IFRS 15 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) and dailyenterprise accounting execution. By examining the alignment between regulatory reportingcriteria and enterprise resource planning software setups, this study outlines a methodology forreducing compliance risk, strengthening internal controls, and improving financial reportingquality in developing economies.Keywords: Financial Reporting, IFRS, IAS 1, IAS 7, IFRS 15, Enterprise Accounting, Compliance, EmergingMarket

title: EMAS Participation in Europe: Organisational and Sectoral Patterns in the Current Register (1995–2025)
summary: ABSTRACT The Eco‐Management and Audit Scheme (EMAS) is a voluntary environmental management scheme that combines management system requirements with external verification and public environmental reporting. Although EMAS was designed as a European instrument, participation remains uneven across countries, sectors and organisation types. This study analyses the current public EMAS register using reported registration years from 1995 to 2025. Because the public register does not provide a complete history of deregistrations or annual historical snapshots, the analysis does not reconstruct the full flow of EMAS adoption and exit over time. Instead, it examines the temporal composition and structural concentration of currently listed EMAS entries. Descriptive statistics, relative country level indicators, contingency tables and sensitivity analyses were used to assess differences by country, NACE activity and employment size class. The analysed dataset included 4333 entries after excluding incomplete 2026 records. Current EMAS entries were strongly concentrated in a small number of countries, with Italy, Germany, Spain, Austria and Slovakia accounting for almost 90% of entries. Sectoral concentration was also evident, especially in waste management, electricity production, construction and public administration. The medium and large organisations dominated the register, whereas micro enterprises remained weakly represented. The employment classes accounted for 60.2%, while the micro class accounted for 10.5%. Counts by reported registration year were highest for 2024 and 2025, at 323 and 391. These descriptive patterns changed little when each registration number was counted once. The findings provide a basis for further research on national differences and organisational capacity, which the register itself cannot explain.

title: LBMNU’s ecological fatwa on mangrove conservation as a religio-legal pathway for localizing SDG 14: Insights from MWCNU Lamongan
summary: Purpose – This article examines how the Bahtsul Masa’il formulation associated with LBM MWCNU Paciran frames mangrove planting as an Islamic legal responsibility and how this locally articulated norm relates to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 14, particularly Target 14.2. Design – The study adopts a qualitative case-study design combining analysis of the institutional document “Rumusan Bahtsul Masa’il Mangrove MWC NU Paciran,” interviews with four participants involved in its formulation and validation, a contemporaneous public report, and relevant scholarly literature. Findings – The institutional formulation classifies mangrove planting as fardlu kifayah and states that the government should establish regulations supporting environmental preservation through mangrove conservation. Interviews illuminate the role of collective responsibility and reasoned fiqh interpretation. The evidence supports normative translation and alignment with SDG Target 14.2, but does not establish community-wide acceptance, policy implementation, or measurable ecological outcomes. Research Implications – The case indicates that religious-legal formulations may provide locally meaningful language for environmental governance. Their practical contribution, however, depends on further evidence of dissemination, stakeholder participation, institutional coordination, policy uptake, and ecological monitoring. Originality – The article distinguishes the production of a local religio-legal norm from its social authorization, implementation, and environmental impact. It thus offers an evidentially bounded account of how a local NU-linked forum can connect Islamic jurisprudence with the normative direction of SDG 14 without equating a written ruling with demonstrated sustainability outcomes.

title: Pengaruh Leverage dan Profitabilitas terhadap Kinerja Corporate Social Responsibility
summary: Penelitian ini menguji pengaruh leverage dan profitabilitas, yang diukur dengan return on equity (ROE), terhadap kinerja corporate social responsibility (CSR). Penelitian ini berfokus pada perusahaan non-keuangan yang terdaftar di Bursa Efek Indonesia (BEI) selama periode 2018–2023. Dengan menggunakan metode purposive sampling, sebanyak 27 perusahaan dipilih sehingga menghasilkan 162 observasi data panel (firm-year observations). Berdasarkan uji Chow, uji Hausman, dan uji Lagrange Multiplier, model yang terpilih adalah random effects model, yang diestimasi menggunakan cluster-robust standard errors pada tingkat perusahaan di STATA. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa ROE berpengaruh positif terhadap kinerja CSR, sedangkan leverage tidak berpengaruh signifikan. Temuan ini mendukung argumen slack resources, yang menunjukkan bahwa perusahaan yang menghasilkan imbal hasil lebih tinggi bagi pemegang saham memiliki kapasitas lebih besar untuk membiayai kegiatan sosial dan lingkungan. Sementara itu, struktur utang tidak memengaruhi kinerja CSR. Hasil ini mengindikasikan bahwa keputusan CSR tidak semata-mata ditentukan oleh kendala pembiayaan, melainkan dapat pula berkaitan dengan kapasitas keuangan perusahaan dan tuntutan pemangku kepentingan (stakeholders). Penelitian ini memberikan bukti mengenai peran profitabilitas dalam mendukung implementasi CSR. Temuan ini dapat menjadi bahan pertimbangan bagi manajemen dalam mengintegrasikan kinerja keuangan dan tanggung jawab sosial ke dalam strategi perusahaan. Selain itu, hasil penelitian ini dapat membantu investor dalam menilai komitmen keberlanjutan perusahaan.

title: The Influence of Tax Approach on Auditor Performance and Value Added Tax (VAT) Compliance through Digital Transformation as a Mediating Variable and Data Quality as a Moderating Variable: An Empirical Study on the Implementation of Coretax
summary: The digital transformation of taxation in Indonesia reaches its peak through the implementation of the Core Tax Administration System (CTAS) or CoreTax. This study examines the impact of the quality of the CoreTax system on voluntary tax compliance and enforced tax compliance, by integrating Tax Authority Legitimacy as a mediating variable and Tax Morale as a moderator. Using an explanatory quantitative design, data were collected from 96 taxpayer respondents in the Special Region of Yogyakarta through purposive sampling techniques and analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling-Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). The research results theoretically synthesize the technical-cognitive and institutional-psychological dimensions to explain the "duality paradigm of compliance." The findings are expected to show that the quality of the system not only functions as an administrative tool but also as a restorer of authority legitimacy. The role of moderating Tax Morale is analyzed as an "amplifier effect" where intrinsic motivation increases taxpayers' sensitivity to the quality of digital services. Practically, this study provides recommendations for the Directorate General of Taxes (DJP) to mitigate the anomalies of bureaucratic digitalization, particularly in balancing technology investments with strengthening public trust to ensure long-term fiscal stability.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Fiduciary Duties: Rethinking Board Liability for Algorithmic Decision-Making
summary: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into corporate decision-making is transforming the traditional structure of corporate governance. From financial forecasting and risk assessment to recruitment, contractual evaluation, fraud detection and strategic planning, AI-driven systems increasingly influence decisions that were historically undertaken by directors and senior management. Although these technologies offer efficiency, predictive accuracy and cost advantages, their deployment raises fundamental questions concerning accountability, transparency, independent judgment and the fiduciary responsibilities of corporate directors. Traditional company law presupposes that directors exercise personal judgment, act in good faith and discharge their responsibilities with reasonable care, skill and diligence. However, algorithmic decision-making complicates this assumption because decisions may be generated through complex systems whose internal reasoning is difficult to interpret, whose training data may contain historical biases and whose outputs may change through continuous learning. The central question is whether directors can discharge their fiduciary obligations merely by relying on technologically sophisticated systems or whether such reliance creates a heightened responsibility to understand, supervise and monitor algorithmic processes. This paper critically examines the relationship between AI-driven corporate decision-making and directors’ fiduciary duties, particularly under Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013. It analyses the emerging challenges of algorithmic opacity, automation bias, accountability gaps, data governance and the delegation of managerial judgment to technological systems. Through comparative examination of the United Kingdom, United States and European Union, the paper evaluates how existing corporate governance principles may be adapted to address AI-related risks. It argues that the adoption of AI does not dilute directors’ legal responsibilities; rather, it requires a more sophisticated interpretation of their duties of care, diligence, good faith and independent judgment. The paper proposes a risk-based framework of AI governance involving board-level oversight, human accountability, algorithmic audits, explainability, continuous monitoring and documented decision-making.

title: Guardians of governance: the role of auditor industry specialization in mitigating corporate misconduct through internal controls
summary: Purpose This study examines the impact of statutory auditor industry specialization on corporate misconduct in China’s A-share market, with a specific focus on the mediating role of internal control quality in mitigating corporate misconduct. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of 3,794 firms (2010-2022), we apply fixed-effects regression models and a two-stage least squares (2SLS) approach to address potential endogeneity. We quantify auditor industry specialization using market share, while the occurrence and frequency of regulatory violations are used to measure corporate misconduct. Findings The results show that auditors with industry specialization significantly reduce both the likelihood and frequency of corporate misconduct. Furthermore, internal control quality serves as a significant mediating mechanism in the relationship between auditor industry specialization and corporate misconduct. These findings highlight the role of industry specialized auditors as vital external governance agents, particularly in firms with concentrated ownership or those operating in highly competitive industries. Practical implications This study highlights policy implications for regulators and policymakers, recommending the development of auditor industry specialization through certification programs and stricter industry-specific auditing standards. Firms should engage industry-specialized auditors and invest in resources and training to improve the quality of internal controls. Originality/value This research significantly contributes to the corporate governance and auditing literature by highlighting that auditor industry specialization serves as a key external disciplinary mechanism that enhances the effectiveness of internal control. It also contributes to agency and resource-based theories by highlighting the critical role of auditor industry specialization and internal control in detecting and preventing corporate misconduct.

title: The Impact of Board Composition on Sustainability Report Readability
summary: This study examines whether and how board composition influences the readability of corporate sustainability reports. Using a sample of 1,334 firm-year observations from S&P 500 companies between 2016 and 2023, we investigate the relationship between board characteristics and report readability while controlling for firm-specific factors. Contrary to conventional wisdom, we find no statistically significant evidence that board-level characteristics, including gender diversity and board size, directly influence sustainability report readability. Our findings suggest that report readability is more likely influenced by operational-level factors than board-level governance structures. These results contribute to the literature on corporate governance and sustainability reporting by challenging existing assumptions about the direct role of board composition in determining reporting quality. Our study has important implications for understanding the mechanisms through which organizational governance affects sustainability disclosure practices.

title: Green upgrades under emission cap regulation
summary: Manufacturers face significant uncertainty regarding green upgrade returns due to strict emission caps and their informational disadvantage relative to retailers. This paper investigates the interplay between emission caps and asymmetric market information in shaping a manufacturer’s green upgrade and pricing decisions. We develop a game-theoretic model of a supply chain where the retailer holds private demand information, resulting in a signalling game via pricing. Our analysis yields three key insights. First, we reveal a regulatory paradox: relaxing strict emission caps can incentivise upgrades by expanding effective capacity and mitigating double marginalisation. Second, information superiority becomes a strategic liability for the retailer. To credibly signal high demand, the retailer is compelled to lower her margin, which erodes her profit but benefits the manufacturer. Third, information asymmetry generates a positive welfare side effect. The retailer’s strategic margin reduction acts as a corrective mechanism for double marginalisation, leading to lower prices and higher social welfare compared to the symmetric information scenario. Our findings suggest that policymakers should balance regulatory stringency with information structures; specifically, moderate regulatory relaxation in information-asymmetric contexts can effectively stimulate corporate green transformation while enhancing market efficiency.

title: Realism or retreat: Unilever weighs the future of purpose
summary: Research methodology The case was prepared entirely from public secondary sources. These include company regulatory filings submitted to the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, Unilever corporate communications and reporting by established business and trade publications. No primary research was conducted, no interviews were held, and no confidential information was used. No information was disguised. Because the case relies only on public sources and does not draw on privileged access to the protagonists, it does not require a signed protagonist release. All factual claims are attributed in the narrative, and quotations are limited to statements already in the public record. Case overview/synopsis For more than a decade, Unilever was regarded as a leader in purpose led business, built on the Sustainable Living Plan launched under chief executive Paul Polman. In April 2024, under new chief executive Hein Schumacher and amid investor pressure, the company scaled back several environmental and social commitments, including its headline plastics and living wage targets, and narrowed its agenda to four priorities. Schumacher framed the change as realism. Less than a year later he stepped down by mutual agreement, and the former chief financial officer, Fernando Fernandez, took charge and sharpened the reset toward a simpler, more focused portfolio. By 2026, the reset met a condition it had not anticipated, as India, Unilever’s second largest market, converted recycled content from ambition into binding law just as the parent company loosened its voluntary targets, leaving Fernandez to set commitments for the next reporting cycle. The case places students at that decision and asks whether a firm’s social and environmental commitments are a defensive strategic asset that protects value in difficult markets, or discretionary spending to be trimmed when returns are demanded. It gives students the evidence to weigh moral capital, the influence of successive chief executives on resource allocation and the role of sustainability in overcoming the liability of foreignness in emerging markets. The case is suited to marketing strategy, corporate social responsibility, strategic management and international business courses. Complexity academic level The case suits upper level undergraduate and master’s students, including MBA students, in marketing strategy, corporate social responsibility and business ethics, strategic management and international business. It works in seated, hybrid and online modalities and fits either a single 90-minute session or an asynchronous discussion. The case has not yet been classroom tested, and authors will report testing results in future revisions.

title: Can CSR/PSCR Survive in Today’s Macro Environment? Lessons Learned from Three Companies: Can Strategically Developed Brand Management Help?
summary: Contemporary culture wars create significant strategic, marketing, brand management, and communication challenges for corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives. Corporate positions on controversial issues can generate stakeholder reactions and reputational risks, requiring carefully developed responses. This paper argues that CSR success depends on integrating corporate values, positions on controversial topics, brand management, organizational responses, and stakeholder communications. Inadequate risk assessment can produce contradictory organizational responses and inconsistent brand management, undermining CSR effectiveness. The literature review examines the emergence of culture wars, their influence on public discourse, and how stakeholders, including customers, social advocates, employees, and government entities, draw companies into these conflicts. Although successful brands are recognized as valuable corporate assets, the paper addresses a gap in understanding when and how brand considerations should inform strategic planning and strategy implementation. Case studies of Disney, Anheuser-Busch, and Victoria’s Secret examine successful and unsuccessful responses to controversial issues. Their experiences provide insights into managing CSR initiatives through effective strategic planning, comprehensive risk assessment, organizational consistency, and coherent brand management to strengthen stakeholder relationships and protect corporate reputation.

title: Stratégie leagile, transformation digitale et incertitude environnementale : vers une compréhension intégrée de la performance des chaînes logistiques
summary: In today’s volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) environment, supply chains are required to balance operational efficiency and responsiveness in order to remain competitive. This study investigates the role of the leagile strategy, a hybrid approach combining lean efficiency and agile responsiveness, in enhancing supply chain performance. Despite growing academic interest, the leagile paradigm remains conceptually fragmented, with limited empirical validation and inconsistent approaches to performance measurement. To address these gaps, this research adopts an exploratory design based on a systematic literature review. Fifty peer-reviewed academic articles published between 2010 and 2025 were selected from major scientific databases in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. A thematic analysis of the selected studies identifies four core dimensions shaping leagile supply chain performance: operational efficiency rooted in lean practices, responsiveness and flexibility driven by agility, digital transformation as an enabling mechanism, and environmental uncertainty as a moderating factor. The findings reveal that leagile performance emerges from a dynamic alignment between these dimensions, allowing supply chains to sustain efficiency while enhancing adaptability in turbulent environments. The study also highlights several theoretical and methodological gaps in the existing literature and outlines directions for future empirical research. From a managerial perspective, the results provide valuable insights for organizations seeking to implement leagile strategies in order to strengthen supply chain resilience, flexibility, and overall performance.

title: Informal Environmental Regulation and Corporate ESG Inconsistency: Evidence From China
summary: ABSTRACT This paper studies whether local informal environmental regulation can limit corporate ESG inconsistency, understood as the gap between what firms disclose about ESG and how they actually perform. Although ESG credibility has attracted growing scholarly attention, evidence remains limited on how community‐based supervision restrains the separation between symbolic disclosure and substantive action. Using Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2010 to 2022, this study finds that stronger local informal regulation is accompanied by a narrower ESG inconsistency gap. The channel tests provide evidence consistent with public attention and pollution‐control investment as potential transmission channels, but do not provide support for the environmental textual emphasis channel. Additional analyses show that the disciplining role of informal regulation depends on the surrounding governance setting: formal enforcement, capital‐market pressure, internal governance arrangements, and negative investor sentiment may dilute the role of social supervision. These findings highlight the macro‐level value of informal environmental regulation in emerging markets. Rather than serving only as a background institutional condition, informal regulation connects public environmental concern, local state response, and corporate ESG accountability. The study contributes to sustainable development and ESG governance research by showing how non‐state pressure can help curb symbolic‐substantive decoupling and strengthen the credibility of corporate sustainability practices.

title: The Feasibility Study as a Financing Prerequisite in Saudi Arabia: A Comparative Review of Development-Fund Requirements and a Practical Framework for Investors
summary: Saudi Arabia channels a large share of project finance for small, medium and industrial enterprises through state development funds and guarantee programmes. Applicants are routinely asked to demonstrate the viability of their project, yet the public documentation of what each financing body expects is fragmented across portals, brochures, press reports and partner-bank pages. This working paper reviews publicly available requirements of five financing channels (the Saudi Industrial Development Fund, the Agricultural Development Fund, the Social Development Bank, the Tourism Development Fund financing programme distributed through a fintech partner, and the national SME loan-guarantee programme) as accessible in November 2026. Using structured document review, it classifies each channel by whether a feasibility study or business case is explicitly required, by the analytical components mentioned, and by the financing parameters disclosed. The review finds that explicit feasibility-study requirements appear mainly in project-type and investment-type financing (industrial competitiveness and acquisition products, specialised agricultural projects), whereas short-term working-capital programmes rely on corporate documents and financial statements. Disclosed financing shares for industrial loans vary by city category (50%, 60% and 75%) with tenors of up to 15 or 20 years. The paper synthesises a nine-component framework for preparing lender-ready feasibility studies in the Saudi context and identifies gaps in public disclosure that applicants should verify directly with each fund. title: INTELLIGENT COST GOVERNANCE IN DIGITAL SUPPLY CHAINS: INTEGRATING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, LOGISTICS OPTIMIZATION, AND MANAGEMENT ACCOUNTING
summary: The increasing complexity of global supply chains necessitates integrated approaches to logistics optimization, financial accountability, and data-driven decision-making. This study proposes an intelligent cost governance framework integrating artificial intelligence (AI), logistics optimization, and management accounting to examine operational performance and its implications for cost management. A quantitative, descriptive-comparative approach is adopted using publicly accessible secondary data, primarily from the World Bank's Logistics Performance Index (LPI) 2023, covering 139 economies. Ten comparative analyses are designed to examine logistics performance across countries, including customs efficiency, infrastructure, international shipments, logistics competence, tracking and tracing, and timeliness. The analysis highlights international differences in logistics capabilities, with Singapore recording an overall LPI score of 4.3 compared with 4.2 for Finland. The proposed framework connects operational indicators with predictive analytics, activity-based costing, and accounting-based performance measurement to identify opportunities for improved cost transparency and resource allocation. The study distinguishes observed logistics performance from unverified financial outcomes, recognizing that country-level data cannot independently establish AI-driven cost savings or causal effects. The research contributes an interdisciplinary framework for linking global logistics benchmarking with intelligent financial decision-making and identifies the additional organizational data necessary to evaluate cost efficiency and financial performance. The findings offer implications for logistics managers, management accountants, and policymakers seeking to strengthen data-driven governance in digital supply chains.

title: Protocol OMEGA-T: QKD-Structured Secure Dissemination Doctrine and Polycrisis Engagement Architecture for Legacy Automotive Governance, Hydrogen Asset Misvaluation, and Climate Lobbying Accountability
summary: This monograph establishes the final execution doctrine and cryptographic dissemination architecture for Protocol "OMEGA-T," an institutional accountability and market-rectification framework targeting structural governance failures, capital misallocation, and obstructive climate lobbying within legacy automotive conglomerates (specifically examining Toyota Motor Corporation and the Toyota Industries buyout valuation dispute). Adopting Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) as both an operational security (OpSec) standard and an information-theoretic doctrine of Perfect Forward Secrecy and source unobservability, this study models how high-integrity evidentiary payloads are routed to high-resonance institutional actors to induce a deterministic polycrisis.The analytical architecture is structured across three strategic quadrants: 1. Media Intelligence (The NYT Triumvirate): Contextual payload tailoring for investigative journalism across technological fraud and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicle (FCV/Mirai) infrastructure collapse (John Carreyrou), systemic climate policy obstruction and InfluenceMap lobbying forensics (Hiroko Tabuchi), and industrial strategy failure amidst global battery electric vehicle (BEV) dominance (Jack Ewing). 2. Capital Market Enforcement (Activist & Institutional Stewardship): Leveraging internal valuation discrepancies, cross-shareholding conflicts of interest, and board independence deficits in the Toyota Industries privatization bid to empower activist intervention (Elliott Investment Management), active asset owners (Hosking Partners), ESG pension funds, and proxy advisors (ISS, Glass Lewis) under fiduciary duty and Caremark oversight standards. 3. Civil Society & Regulatory Accountability: Synchronizing empirical lobbying disclosures with NGO scorecards (InfluenceMap, Lead the Charge, Public Citizen, Sierra Club) to quantify the social and environmental costs of regulatory delay. Finally, the monograph specifies a zero-footprint cryptographic logistics sequence utilizing Tails OS, Tor-routed SecureDrop onion endpoints, MAT2 metadata sanitization, and linguistic stylometry flattening, ensuring mathematically verifiable payload authenticity alongside absolute source anonymity.

title: Risk and resilience strategies in global supply chains: evidence from a mixed-methods analysis
summary: Purpose This study aims to investigate how manufacturing small and medium enterprises embedded in global supply chains manage systemic disruptions, including geopolitical crises, pandemics and environmental shocks. It identifies three vulnerability mechanisms – dependence on internationally sourced inputs, limited knowledge of input origins and difficulty substituting critical inputs – and examines how these mechanisms shape resilience strategies. Design/methodology/approach This study uses an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. A survey of 465 small and medium enterprises was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling to examine the relationships between supply chain vulnerabilities and crisis impacts. The qualitative phase drew on an expert panel and two focus groups with small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) managers and supply chain experts to explain and extend the quantitative results. The two phases were integrated into a conceptual framework linking vulnerability mechanisms, strategic responses and resilience. Findings Quantitative results show that dependence on internationally sourced inputs is positively associated with disruption impacts, including among SMEs characterized by limited upstream visibility and difficult-to-substitute inputs. The qualitative analysis explains how small and medium enterprises mitigate these vulnerabilities through strategic shifts, collaborative practices and process adaptation. It further shows that upstream visibility, diversified sourcing options, supplier collaboration and dynamic planning shape SMEs’ ability to respond to disruptions, subject to financial, technical, relational and temporal constraints. Research limitations/implications The findings are based on Canadian manufacturing small and medium enterprises and may not generalize directly to other sectors or national contexts. Cross-sectoral and cross-country research is therefore needed to assess the external validity of the proposed relationships. Practical implications This study provides small and medium enterprise managers with practical strategies to strengthen resilience, including supplier diversification, investment in supply chain mapping and collaborative risk management. These insights help small and medium enterprises transform vulnerability into adaptive capacity, improving preparedness for future systemic disruptions. Originality/value This study extends supply chain resilience research to small and medium enterprises, a group often overlooked compared to large firms. By integrating risk management, contingency theory and dynamic capabilities, this study introduces an original framework explaining how vulnerabilities and capabilities interact to enable resilience under systemic crises.

title: Retail Environmental Responsibility and the Consumer Waste Behaviour Gap: Evidence from South Africa
summary: Abstract Retailers sit between production and household consumption, which makes their environmental corporate social responsibility programmes plausible instruments of behavioural change. Whether customer recognition of those programmes translates into waste management behaviour remains unclear in secondary cities of the global South, where recovery infrastructure is uneven. We surveyed 281 adult customers at two retail complexes in Mbombela, Mpumalanga, South Africa. The questionnaire measured awareness of environmental CSR, information channels, noticed initiatives, perceived effectiveness, perceived influence on waste behaviour, reported household recycling, participation in store led recovery schemes, changes in shopping practice, and barriers to sustainable consumption. We screened the captured data against the permitted response codes, decomposed multiple response items into binary indicators, and used Spearman rank correlations with Benjamini and Hochberg correction for 66 pairwise tests. Awareness was reported by 194 of 279 interpretable respondents, or 69.5%. However, only 75 respondents, or 26.7%, reported recycling household waste, and 147 of 281 reported regular or occasional participation in store led recovery schemes. Among respondents giving an interpretable answer, 187 of 228, or 82.0% believed that retailer initiatives had influenced their waste behaviour. Awareness was associated with perceived influence, but not with household recycling and store scheme participation. Education and age were more consistent correlates of scheme participation, while perceived barriers were more salient among respondents who reported greater engagement. The findings indicate that retailer CSR can be highly visible and persuasive at the level of perception without being sufficient to produce downstream waste behaviour. Consumer communication therefore needs to be coupled to accessible collection, sorting, and recovery systems.

title: CREDIT RISK MANAGEMENT IN FACTORING AND SUPPLY CHAIN FINANCE: A BIBLIOMETRIC ANALYSIS OF SCIENTIFIC PUBLICATIONS
summary: Factoring and supply chain finance (SCF) allow firms, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, to obtain liquidity against receivables and other trade assets, but they expose financiers to the credit risk of suppliers, buyers and their relationships. This study maps the scientific literature on credit risk management in factoring and SCF through a bibliometric analysis. A Scopus search conducted on 12 October 2026 and screening following the PRISMA 2020 flow yielded 288 articles and reviews published between 1995 and 2025. Performance analysis was combined with science mapping in VOSviewer, including keyword co-occurrence, country co-authorship and co-citation analyses of references and sources. The results show that the field has grown rapidly since 2019, with 87.2% of the documents published in 2019–2025. China dominates research output, while studies from the United Kingdom, the United States and Italy attain higher normalised impact, and operations management and operational research journals are the main publication venues. Three research streams are identified: analytical operations–finance models of risk allocation in capital-constrained supply chains, conceptual and empirical research on SCF adoption and reverse factoring, and machine learning-based credit risk assessment of SMEs. Research attention has shifted from traditional factoring and receivables financing towards SCF, machine learning, blockchain and, most recently, artificial intelligence and sustainability. The accounting, financial reporting and internal control dimensions of these arrangements, the allocation of risk among multiple financiers, and evidence from under-represented regions emerge as the main gaps.

title: When Stable Systems Remain Wrong: Identifiability, Detection and Correction of Shared Error in a Minimal Multi-Agent Feedback Model; Wenn stabile Systeme falsch bleiben: Identifizierbarkeit, Erkennung und Korrektur gemeinsamer Fehler in einem minimalen Multi-Agenten-Rückkopplungsmodell
summary: Description / Abstract English When Stable Systems Remain Wrong: Identifiability, Detection and Correction of Shared Error in a Minimal Multi-Agent Feedback Model Version 0.4.2 | Research Preprint | 8 November 2026 Author: Dipl.-Ing. Bernd von MallinckrodtResearch Programme: BenchEWS Background and Research Question Can a system remain stable while systematically producing incorrect decisions? Under what conditions can it recognize, identify and correct its own errors? This study investigates these questions using a minimal multi-agent feedback model based on Friedkin–Johnsen-type opinion dynamics, quality-weighted information aggregation and competing correction architectures. The central distinction is between stability, identifiability, detectability, correctability and actual correction performance. Methods The study combines established mathematical results with computational experiments: Formal analysis of shared-error identifiability, observation limits and correction constraints. Eight pre-specified hypotheses tested across 141 independently generated networks and 320 experimental variants. Statistical evaluation using network-level comparisons and bootstrap confidence intervals. Exploratory sensitivity analyses and robustness investigations. A prospectively specified exploratory follow-up experiment (X3), comparing an observation-based correction strategy with existing audit architectures and an oracle benchmark. Reproducibility documentation, executable code and supplementary verification materials. Principal Findings 1. Stability does not guarantee correctness.A feedback system can converge to a stable equilibrium while maintaining a systematic collective error. 2. Shared errors may be fundamentally unidentifiable.When all accessible information channels contain the same unknown bias, internal observations alone cannot distinguish that bias from the true state under the specified assumptions. 3. Detecting an error does not guarantee the ability to correct it.Even identifiable errors may remain uncorrectable within a restricted class of interventions. 4. Influence matters more than numerical majority alone.Within the simulated model, a highly influential minority produced greater decision errors than a larger majority with limited influence. 5. Correction mechanisms can amplify errors.Auditing against biased or compromised references may perform worse than conducting no audit. 6. Observation-based correction can substantially improve performance under favorable information conditions.In exploratory experiment X3, an admissible reweighting strategy reduced late absolute error from 0.528 to 0.175, approaching the implemented oracle benchmark of 0.174 within statistical uncertainty. This result depends on the simulated model and honest reference information. 7. Negative findings are explicitly reported.The structural indicator Φ did not demonstrate incremental discrimination beyond variance and lag-1 autocorrelation in the tested classification setting. Scientific Contribution The principal contribution is not a new mathematical theorem but an integrated framework distinguishing: Information limits Algorithmic correction gaps Information gaps within an intervention class Residual errors caused by actuator constraints The accompanying computational benchmark provides a reproducible environment for investigating when systems can recognize and correct their own mistakes. Limitations and Scientific Status All empirical evidence is synthetic. The mathematical results rely on established principles applied to the specified model. The study does not demonstrate effectiveness in real societies, organizations, biological systems or engineered applications. Mathematical verification, computational reimplementations and literature assessment were performed within an AI-assisted research workflow. Independent human peer review and external replication remain outstanding. This publication is therefore presented as a research preprint, not as an independently validated empirical demonstration. Supplementary Materials The release includes English and German manuscripts, mathematical and statistical appendices, computational materials, simulation results and reproducibility documentation.
