title: Digital Transformation in Sustainable Building Design: User Perspectives on Architectural Tools and Applications
summary: Digital transformation is increasingly reshaping sustainable building design by enhancing innovation, accuracy, and productivity through advanced digital tools. This study investigates how users’ self-reported familiarity with perceptions and use of modeling, simulation, and artificial intelligence (AI) applications contribute to sustainability-oriented design practices. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was adopted, informed by a narrative review of the literature. The survey targeted students, academics, and recent graduates in architectural engineering. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, ranking analysis, and Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) to examine digital competency patterns and tool evaluation criteria. The results reveal a common dimension of self-reported digital familiarity and proficiency across modeling, simulation, and AI applications, highlighting the importance of hybrid digital skillsets in sustainability-oriented workflows. Modeling, simulation, and AI applications collectively contribute to a unified competency dimension, highlighting the importance of hybrid digital skillsets. While traditional modeling tools demonstrate stable and widely shared perceptions regarding accuracy and productivity, AI-based tools exhibit more heterogeneous perceptions across functional categories. The second MFA dimension was more strongly associated with modeling than with simulation or AI, without establishing distinct specialization pathways. This study emphasizes the need for integrated digital workflows and competency-based education to support sustainable design. It contributes empirical evidence to the understanding of digital transformation in architectural practice and highlights emerging challenges and opportunities associated with AI integration.

title: Becoming Digital: Lecturers’ Meaning-Making of Digital Transformation in Islamic Higher Education
summary: Digital transformation in higher education changes academic work as well as institutional systems, raising questions about how lecturers interpret its benefits and demands. This study examines how lecturers at Universitas Islam Negeri Sulthan Thaha Saifuddin Jambi, Indonesia, experience, interpret, and negotiate digital transformation in their academic work. Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis was employed, drawing primarily on semi-structured interviews with ten lecturers, supplemented by observation and document review. Analysis proceeded through repeated reading, initial noting, within-case theme development, and cross-case interpretation. Five interrelated themes concerned acceptance of digitalization alongside application fragmentation, adaptation through collective learning, negotiation of digital demands against academic workload, changing work culture, and the preservation of academic purpose. The fifth theme connected the others through lecturers’ judgments about whether technology supported their professional responsibilities. The findings are synthesized as negotiated becoming digital: lecturers’ ongoing incorporation of institutional digital requirements while evaluating and adjusting their implications for meaningful academic work. This situated interpretation connects participation in modernization with practical efforts to preserve professional priorities. The findings suggest that institutional managers should examine overlapping workflows, provide continuing technical and peer support, and evaluate digital initiatives through their contribution to academic responsibilities. The study offers an interpretive contribution from one Islamic university rather than a general model of digital transformation

title: Fintech and the Profitability of Deposit Money Banks in Nigeria
summary: This study empirically examines the effect of Financial Technology (Fintech) adoption on the profitability of Deposit Money Banks (DMBs) in Nigeria over a 26-year period from 2000 to 2025. Adopting an ex-post facto research design, secondary time-series data were compiled from Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Statistical Bulletins, Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS) reports, and bank financial statements. Bank profitability was operationalised using Return on Assets (ROA), while Fintech adoption was disaggregated into three core transaction channels: Mobile Banking Transaction Value (LnMBTV), Point-of-Sale Transaction Value (LnPOSTV), and Web/Internet Banking Transaction Value (LnWIBTV). Employing Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) multiple regression analysis alongside rigorous diagnostic and stationarity tests, the empirical results reveal that Mobile Banking Transaction Value and Web/Internet Banking Transaction Value exert positive and statistically significant effects on bank profitability (ROA). Conversely, Point of Sale Transaction Value demonstrated a negative and statistically insignificant impact, largely attributable to high terminal acquisition expenses, maintenance overheads, and aggregator cost-sharing structures. The overall model yielded an R2 of 0.5842 and an F-statistic of 10.3082 (p < 0.01), confirming robust explanatory power. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Innovation Diffusion Theory, and the Resource-Based View (RBV), the study concludes that digital banking channels are vital drivers of asset efficiency and fee-based income. The research recommends strategic investments in mobile infrastructure and cybersecurity, paired with cost optimisation and restructuring of aggregator fees for POS networks, to maximise net profitability gains from digital financial services in Nigeria.

title: The Impact of Digital Audit and Artificial Intelligence on the Field of Audit
summary: Digitalization, big data and artificial intelligence (AI) are shifting auditing from periodic, sample-based verification towards data-driven procedures that can cover entire populations of transactions. This article examines the conceptual foundations of digital auditing, the opportunities and limitations of AI in audit practice, and the institutional environment that is emerging in Azerbaijan. The study combines a structured review of peer-reviewed literature, documentary and normative-legal analysis, and a comparative review of publicly described Big Four audit platforms (Deloitte Omnia, PwC Halo, EY Helix, KPMG Clara). It assesses how recent national developments—the Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2025–2028 (Presidential Order No. 530 of 19 March 2025), the Regulation on the “Digital State Finance” Information System (RDMİS) approved by Presidential Decree No. 590 of 26 January 2026, and the “State Audit” Information System (DAİS) established by Presidential Decree No. 768 of 14 August 2026—relate to international requirements, including ISA 315 (Revised 2019), ISA 240 (Revised) and the 2024 PCAOB amendments to AS 1105 and AS 2301. The findings suggest that Azerbaijan is building the data infrastructure required for analytics-based public-sector audit, while audit-specific AI governance, auditor competence and data-protection safeguards remain open issues. A balanced, principles-based approach to regulation is proposed.

title: How Are Business Strategy and ESG Performance Associated With Stock Liquidity? Global Insights
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines whether business strategy is associated with stock liquidity and whether environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance conditions this association. Using 58,638 firm‐year observations from 74 countries during 2008–2023, we find no significant association for the continuous strategy score. In categorical analyses, Defender firms exhibit higher illiquidity and Analyzer firms lower illiquidity, both at the 10% significance level, while no reliable average association is found for Prospectors. ESG performance is associated with lower illiquidity in the continuous‐score specification. Marginal‐effects analysis shows that ESG moderates these relationships asymmetrically: higher ESG reduces the Defender illiquidity disadvantage but attenuates the Analyzer liquidity advantage, while the Prospector marginal effect remains insignificant across observed ESG levels. The principal strategy‐specific and interaction patterns are broadly robust across alternative liquidity measures, lagged specifications, crisis‐period exclusions, country‐sample restrictions, log‐transformed illiquidity, and supplementary System GMM estimates.

title: Mapping data privacy at the intersection of AI and the digital economy: a bibliometric review, taxonomy, and research agenda
summary: Abstract The rapid integration of artificial intelligence and related emerging technologies has intensified data privacy challenges across the digital economy. Although scholarship has grown substantially, it remains fragmented across technical, legal, ethical, and sector-specific domains, limiting a clear view of the field’s structure and development. This study presents a bibliometric analysis and thematic mapping of 434 peer-reviewed articles published between 2016 and 2026 in the Web of Science Core Collection. It identifies seven thematic clusters and finds that applied and privacy-preserving technical work dominates, while business strategy, trust, and public-sector governance remain underdeveloped. The study extends this mapping with a multi-dimensional privacy taxonomy and a TCCM (theory, context, characteristics, and methodology) synthesis, moving beyond the topic- and domain-specific scope of prior reviews to diagnose where the field is structurally weak. It argues that privacy remains under-theorized as an economic and behavioral phenomenon despite its centrality to digital commerce and sets out a research agenda of economically grounded questions derived from these gaps.

title: Carbon risk, accounting conservatism and the moderating role of financial materiality adoption: international evidence
summary: Purpose This paper aims to investigate the direct effect of carbon risk on conditional accounting conservatism and examine the moderating role of the adoption of the financial materiality (FM) principle. Design/methodology/approach This study conducts multivariate regression analysis on a panel of 315 firms from high-emission sectors across 17 countries (2020–2024), drawing on the Refinitiv Eikon and Bloomberg databases. Findings The results indicate that carbon risk has a negative effect on conditional conservatism. FM further amplifies this negative relationship. As this reporting principle is intended to enhance transparency and promote the timely recognition of carbon risk, the finding may be consistent with its symbolic implementation. Robustness checks show that external assurance of environmental disclosures neither mitigates this delayed recognition nor attenuates the amplifying effect of FM. The findings remain robust under alternative measures and after addressing potential endogeneity concerns. Originality/value This study offers post-2020 evidence on the relationship between carbon risk and conditional conservatism, addressing a literature that remains limited, mixed and largely rooted in earlier regulatory contexts. Moreover, whereas prior research has primarily examined FM’s implications for non-financial disclosure, this study shifts attention to its unintended consequences for accounting prudence. The results offer policy-relevant implications for highly polluting firms, auditors and investors amid the growing salience of corporate carbon risk.

title: Financial Crises and Corporate Sustainability: A Comparative Analysis of Shariah-Compliant and Non-Shariah-Compliant Firms. Evidence from the Global Financial Crisis and COVID-19
summary: Purpose – This study examines the relationship between financial crises and corporate sustainability by comparing Shariah-compliant and non-Shariah-compliant firms. It focuses on two major crises, the 2008 Global Financial Crisis (GFC) and COVID-19, to evaluate how resilient these firms were in periods of crisis. Design/Methodology/Approach – The study uses a longitudinal dataset covering 2004–2023, drawn from the Thomson Reuters ESG database, and applies panel data regression models (OLS, fixed effects, random effects and feasible generalized least squares). Corporate sustainability is measured through environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance, and the effect of Shariah compliance on it is evaluated. Findings – Shariah-compliant firms show greater resilience during financial crises, which is linked to their ethical investment practices, risk-sharing mechanisms and stakeholder-oriented governance. Shariah-compliant firms performed relatively better during the GFC. During COVID-19, however, non-compliant firms adopted adaptive strategies and strengthened their ESG commitments. Originality/Value – The findings add to the literature on financial stability and sustainable finance by highlighting the role of ethical financial practices in promoting corporate sustainability. The study offers useful information to policy makers, investors and corporate leaders on integrating sustainable financial models to build resilience against future economic crises.

title: Capital Market Depth, Technological Advancement, and Entrepreneurial Activity in Europe: A Calibrated Simulation Study of Curvilinear and Contingent Effects
summary: European policymakers have paired the Capital Markets Union agenda with large public investments in technological advancement, yet the joint consequences of these two levers for entrepreneurship remain poorly understood. This study develops and tests a framework in which capital market depth shapes how technology development translates into entrepreneurial activity. Drawing on finance-and-growth theory, the knowledge spillover theory of entrepreneurship, and the too-much-of-a-good-thing perspective, we argue that technology development has an inverted U-shaped relationship with new venture entry and that deep capital markets shift the turning point outward and flatten the downturn. At the venture level, we argue that capital market depth amplifies the growth returns to venture-level technological advancement, particularly in munificent task environments. We evaluate these predictions using a calibrated two-level simulation of 4,500 country-industry-years across 30 European economies and 14,000 new ventures, combining two-way fixed effects, instrumental variables, formal turning-point tests, and a 216-specification multiverse analysis. The inverted U holds where capital markets are shallow or average but disappears where they are deep, and the venture-level interaction is robust for growth but not for survival. The study offers a transparent, replicable design for future work with administrative European data.

title: GHG, SDGs, ESG, IPCC, CCC and All the Letters of the Climate Alphabet: Environmental and Social Benefits of Climate Planning Through the Mobilization of the Private Sector
summary: Mission-oriented transitions require governments to shape markets and co-create value with private actors, yet municipal and private actors assess climate action through different categories. Cities and regions use climate action plans, greenhouse-gas (GHG) inventories and reporting platforms; companies and investors use environmental, social and governance (ESG) frameworks, including the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), the EU Taxonomy, the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR), and bond principles. This thematic review analyzes key frameworks and maps their subcategories across emissions domains, climate risk, investment and financing, and social benefits. It uses transition design as an organizing lens by mapping alignment and relationships among sectoral actions, finance, governance and social outcomes at a systemic level. Responding to needs emerging from the Mission Cities, this paper proposes a project-level shared language structured as a boundary object to enhance municipal–private sector mutual understanding, thereby supporting capacity building, decision making and collaboration. The analysis identifies where standards, including the ESRS, the EU Taxonomy and the SFDR, can be transferred or translated to the emissions domains of energy, buildings, mobility and hazards, and where more integration work is needed, notably on social benefits.

title: Inverse Fintech: Nineteen Claims for Debate: A Discussion Note
summary: This discussion note puts nineteen propositions about Inverse Fintech forward for academic and public debate. Inverse Fintech is a proposed economic and financial framework in which access to productive assets precedes, rather than depends upon, conventional creditworthiness. At its centre lies a proposed economic transformation: while a physical asset depreciates over time, the verified information generated through its productive use may progressively appreciate in economic and institutional value. The propositions are ordered from the least to the most contestable, in four tiers: descriptive and definitional statements (Tier 1), plausible premises drawn from the economics of information and networks (Tier 2), hypotheses about causal mechanisms to be tested empirically (Tier 3), and normative positions on the distribution of risk and value (Tier 4). None is presented as an established empirical finding. Readers are invited to identify the first proposition they reject and to state why. The author welcomes collaboration with researchers and students, particularly in development economics, finance and information economics, to examine, challenge and further develop the framework. This note is the fourth work in the Inverse Fintech series, following the definition paper (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24046147), the explanatory paper (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24056786) and the research prospectus (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24063432).

title: THE IMPACT OF FINTECH TOOLS ON THE TRANSFORMATION OF THE FINANCIAL INVESTMENT MARKET
summary: The article examines how FinTech tools transform the structure, accessibility and operating mechanisms of the financial investment market. The study proceeds from the premise that digitalisation is changing not only the technical channel through which an investor buys a financial asset, but also the architecture of intermediation, the cost of investment services, portfolio formation, information processing and the distribution of risks between investors, platforms and regulated financial institutions. The main groups of investment-oriented FinTech tools are systematised: mobile investment platforms, robo-advisory, artificial-intelligence-based analytics, open banking and API infrastructure, distributed-ledger solutions and asset tokenisation. Recent academic evidence indicates that automated advice can broaden access to professional portfolio management, improve diversification for some self-directed investors and reduce the time and fees associated with portfolio management. At the same time, digital investment environments generate new risks related to algorithmic bias, data quality, cybersecurity, opaque decision models, gamification, digital nudging, conflicts of interest and the rapid diffusion of unreliable investment content through social networks. The paper proposes an author's four-contour model of FinTech transformation of the financial investment market. It combines technological, institutional, behavioural and regulatory dimensions and demonstrates that sustainable digitalisation requires their coordinated development. Particular attention is paid to Ukraine, where the legal framework for payment services and the introduction of open banking create a technological basis for a more integrated digital financial ecosystem. It is argued that the next stage should connect open-finance infrastructure with regulated investment services, strengthen digital investor protection, develop RegTech/SupTech mechanisms and promote digital financial literacy. The practical significance of the results lies in using the proposed framework when designing digital investment products, regulatory approaches and educational components for finance specialists.

title: Strategic human resource management, open innovation, and digital transformation for perceived sustainable university performance
summary: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractHigher education institutions are increasingly expected to achieve sustainable performance amid rapid technological and societal change. However, the organizational capability mechanisms through which strategic human resource management (strategic HRM) contributes to perceived sustainable university performance remain insufficiently understood, particularly in developing-country contexts. This study examines the relationships among strategic HRM, open innovation, digital transformation, and perceived sustainable university performance in Thai higher education institutions. A quantitative cross-sectional survey involved 440 academic and administrative personnel from 110 higher education institutions. Because employees were the unit of analysis, all constructs were measured as employee perceptions. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with a two-stage hierarchical component model and 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Strategic HRM was positively associated with open innovation (β = 0.540), digital transformation (β = 0.752), and perceived sustainable university performance (β = 0.296). Digital transformation was positively associated with perceived sustainable university performance (β = 0.604), whereas open innovation was positively associated with digital transformation (β = 0.166) but not directly with perceived sustainable university performance (β = −0.022, p = 0.541). The model explained 29.2%, 72.7%, and 73.1% of the variance in open innovation, digital transformation, and perceived sustainable university performance, respectively. Digital transformation significantly mediated the strategic HRM–performance relationship, while sequential mediation through open innovation and digital transformation was also significant. The findings extend the resource-based view and dynamic capability theory by demonstrating complementary capability mechanisms associated with sustainability perceptions in higher education.

title: The Integrated Effect of Quality and Maintenance Management on Sustainability in Saudi Manufacturing: Implications for Industrial Digital Transformation
summary: Industrial digital transformation in manufacturing requires more than technology deployment; it also depends on organizational routines that coordinate process discipline, workforce learning, and asset reliability. Drawing on Dynamic Capabilities Theory, this study examines how Total Quality Management (TQM) and Total Productive Maintenance (TPM) jointly contribute to economic, environmental, and social sustainability in Saudi food manufacturing, with TPM modeled as an operational mediator. Survey data were collected from 470 distinct food manufacturing organizations across Saudi Arabia between December 2025 and February 2026. A reflective–formative higher-order model was estimated in SmartPLS 4 with the disjoint two-stage approach, 5000 bootstrap resamples, heterotrait–monotrait (HTMT) assessment with bootstrap confidence intervals, and importance–performance map analysis (IPMA). TQM positively affected sustainability performance (β = 0.327, p < 0.001) and predicted TPM (β = 0.592, p < 0.001); TPM, in turn, positively affected sustainability performance (β = 0.534, p < 0.001). The indirect TQM → TPM → sustainability pathway was significant (β = 0.316, 95% CI [0.274, 0.369]), indicating complementary partial mediation; the total effect of TQM on sustainability performance was 0.643. The model explained 59.8% of the variance in overall sustainability performance and 35.0% of the variance in TPM. IPMA identified safety, health and environment, self-maintenance, learning and creativity, and process management as recurring managerial priorities, with human-resource practices emerging as the leading priority for environmental performance. These findings position TQM–TPM integration as an organizational and human-capability foundation for sustainable industrial transformation: quality routines create the conditions for coordinated improvement, while maintenance capability translates them into reliable asset-centered practice. Because the study did not measure digital technology adoption or digital maturity, its contribution to industrial digital transformation is capability- and readiness-oriented rather than an estimate of the effects of specific digital technologies.

title: Inverse Fintech: From economic proposition to practical application. An explanatory paper on the WeSail.Green model
summary: Inverse Fintech This paper explains the term Inverse Fintech: an asset-first approach to financial inclusion in which access to a deliberately selected productive asset is used to help create the repayment capacity and the financial record that conventional lending requires in advance. It sets out the definition, positions the idea against the Graduation approach, pay-as-you-go digital collateral and alternative-data credit scoring, and describes a six-layer architecture of productive asset, capability, fair finance, household protection, evidence and graduation, governed throughout by consent, privacy and independent evaluation. It traces the idea to the author's hire-purchase experience in Uganda (1997–2006), including the lessons of the Shimoni litigation, and explains how WeSail.Green proposes to test it in a 300-household pilot in Kenya, illustrates the economics with one household followed through the full contract, and shows how location and generation evidence may continue to serve carbon accounting, regional energy planning and the stewardship of second-life panels after the contract ends. The paper states what the pilot can and cannot establish. No Kenyan outcome data yet exist.

title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN HEALTHCARE MANAGEMENT: EVALUATING HOSPITAL PRODUCTIVITY, PATIENT EXPERIENCE, AND CLINICAL DECISION PERFORMANCE
summary: Digital transformation has emerged as a significant driver of healthcare modernization, influencing hospital productivity, patient experience, clinical decision-making, and overall institutional performance. The integration of electronic health records (EHRs), artificial intelligence (AI), telemedicine, clinical decision support systems (CDSS), and hospital information management systems has created new opportunities to improve healthcare service delivery and administrative efficiency. This study aims to evaluate the influence of digital transformation on three critical dimensions of healthcare management: hospital productivity, patient experience, and clinical decision performance. The proposed research adopts a quantitative comparative approach using publicly available healthcare datasets, published empirical studies, and institutional performance indicators. The evaluation focuses on measurable parameters, including patient waiting time, hospital bed utilization, average length of stay, administrative processing time, patient satisfaction, clinical decision accuracy, diagnostic efficiency, and healthcare operational costs. Numerical comparison tables are used to examine performance differences across digital adoption levels, healthcare technologies, and institutional settings. The analytical framework also considers the relationships between digital infrastructure, managerial efficiency, clinical workflow integration, and patient-centred healthcare delivery. Particular attention is given to identifying the operational benefits and implementation challenges associated with digital healthcare technologies, including interoperability limitations, data security concerns, workforce readiness, and technological investment requirements. The study is designed to consolidate evidence on the extent to which digital transformation contributes to improved hospital management, enhanced patient engagement, and more effective clinical decision-making. The final analysis will identify measurable performance differences, technology-specific contributions, and managerial implications based on verified numerical evidence. The research seeks to provide an evidence-based framework to support healthcare administrators, hospital managers, policymakers, and clinical professionals in evaluating digital investments and developing sustainable healthcare transformation strategies.

title: Family coordination and digital transformation: resilience and post-COVID reinvention in Saudi micro and small family enterprises
summary: Purpose This study aims to explain how family-based coordination resources support post-crisis change by distinguishing organizational resilience from post-crisis reinvention. It tests whether family embeddedness, family labour reliance and informal family governance predict later resilience and whether digitalization strengthens the resilience−reinvention relationship in Saudi micro and small family enterprises. Design/methodology/approach A two-wave survey with an exact 70-day individual lag produced an analytic sample of 318 firms. Time 1 measured family resources, digitalization, COVID shock severity and baseline outcomes; Time 2 measured resilience and reinvention. Primary models in Mplus 8.10 used MLR, FIML and autoregressive controls. Indirect-effect intervals came from a separate 5,000-replication ML bootstrap, and the latent resilience x digitalization interaction was estimated separately under TYPE = RANDOM. Findings All three family resources were positively associated with Time 2 resilience, but their direct paths to reinvention were small and nonsignificant. Their indirect associations through resilience were significant. Resilience and digitalization were positively associated with reinvention, and the resilience−reinvention relationship strengthened as digitalization increased. Because resilience and reinvention were contemporaneous at Time 2, the conditional indirect pattern is interpreted associationally. Originality/value This study develops a staged conditional-process explanation: family resources supply coordination capacity for continuity, while digitalization strengthens the conversion of preserved capacity into renewal. The Saudi setting makes this mechanism theoretically salient because kin-based coordination and informal governance coexist with institutional modernization and rapid SME digitalization.

title: FROM DECLARED ORIGIN TO TERRITORIAL VERIFICATION: RELATIONAL TRACING AND GOVERNANCE IN AN ARTISANAL PEQUI (Caryocar spp.) OIL SUPPLY CHAIN IN BRAZIL
summary: Artisanal non-timber forest product chains often reach urban markets without documentary records, limiting verification of provenance, producer participation, and product trajectories. This study examines how fragmented commercial information can support the exploratory reconstruction of supply relationships in an artisanal pequi (Caryocar spp.) oil chain and identify opportunities for greater transparency. Documentary review, official statistical and institutional databases, direct observation, and relational tracing were combined across 89 sales points in four public markets and the Teresina Wholesale Supply Center in Piauí, northeastern Brazil. Twenty-nine sales points reported selling pequi oil. Seventeen provided territorial references or interstate commercial-route information, including 12 references to localities within Piauí and five references to external territories or interstate routes. Five identified suppliers or redistribution channels without a production location, and seven provided neither a declared origin nor a traceable supply connection. Institutional mediation enabled territorial access to Boa Hora, while independent confirmation of a specific producer-supplier relationship verified one productive linkage to the urban commercial circuit. All other reported origins remained unverified commercial claims. Provenance information was unevenly distributed among vendors, intermediaries, institutions, and producing territories. Intermediation supported market access and redistribution but concentrated information at particular nodes, reducing downstream producer visibility while supplying leads for territorial verification. The study proposes declared origin as an evidentiary category between missing provenance and documentary traceability and relational tracing as a potentially transferable exploratory method for under-documented forest-product chains. Governance should preserve minimum product and provenance information across transactions without shifting disproportionate compliance burdens to women extractivists and other small-scale producers.

title: Linking Principals’ Digital Leadership to Teacher Performance through Digital Transformation Readiness: An Integrative Literature Review
summary: Digital transformation has reshaped educational practices and increased the need for school leadership that can support teachers in adapting to technology-driven changes. However, existing studies tend to examine principals’ digital leadership, teacher readiness, and teacher performance separately, leaving the mechanism connecting these constructs insufficiently integrated. This study aims to synthesize existing evidence on the relationships among principals’ digital leadership, teachers’ digital transformation readiness, and teacher performance, and to develop an integrative framework explaining the potential role of readiness in linking leadership with professional performance. An integrative literature review was conducted using a predefined corpus of 12 scholarly articles published between 2022 and 2026. The articles were examined through structured evidence extraction, evidence classification, conceptual harmonization, relational synthesis, and integrative thematic synthesis. The findings show relatively consistent evidence that principals’ digital leadership is positively associated with teacher performance, while complementary evidence indicates relationships between digital leadership and digital readiness and between readiness for change and teacher performance. The synthesis further identifies teacher digital transformation readiness as a multidimensional construct encompassing capability readiness, psychological readiness, and organizationally enabled readiness. Nevertheless, none of the reviewed studies directly tested the complete pathway linking principals’ digital leadership to teacher performance through digital transformation readiness. Therefore, this review proposes digital transformation readiness as a theoretically plausible explanatory mechanism rather than an empirically confirmed mediator. The resulting leadership–readiness–performance framework highlights that effective educational digital transformation depends on the interaction between supportive digital leadership, teachers’ preparedness for change, and enabling organizational conditions.

title: A Comparative Analysis of the Fintech Industry and Regulatory Frameworks in Indonesia and Malaysia
summary: The rapid growth of financial technology (fintech), particularly in digital payment services, has revolutionized financial transactions worldwide. Across Asia, Malaysia and Indonesia have emerged as key players in harnessing fintech to enhance financial inclusion, improve efficiency, and modernize their economies. Although they share these objectives, the two countries’ development trajectories and regulatory frameworks differ substantially because of variations in their economic structures, levels of technological adoption, and regulatory practices. This study examines the fintech industries of Malaysia and Indonesia, with particular emphasis on their digital payment ecosystems, prevalent payment methods, and regulatory approaches, including frameworks for Islamic fintech. Drawing on an extensive review of academic literature and regulatory policies, this comparative analysis provides insights into strategic decisions that both countries could consider to enhance their fintech ecosystems and regulatory frameworks. The findings may serve as a guide for Indonesian and Malaysian policymakers and industry stakeholders seeking to establish resilient and inclusive fintech ecosystems supported by robust regulatory frameworks.

title: Impact of Audit Quality on Fraud Prevention in Quoted Deposit Money Banks in Nigeria
summary: Fraud remains a persistent challenge in Nigeria’s banking sector, particularly among quoted deposit money banks (DMBs), despite stringent regulatory oversight and internal control mechanisms. Weak audit quality has been identified as a critical factor that can exacerbate the risk of fraudulent activities, undermining stakeholder confidence and financial integrity. The main objective of this study was to examine the impact of audit quality on fraud prevention in Nigerian quoted DMBs, focusing specifically on three dimensions of audit quality: auditor competence, auditor independence, and audit evidence quality. The study employed a combined ex-post-facto and survey research design, collecting primary data from 70 respondents across 14 listed deposit money banks as of December 31, 2025. Census sampling was used to ensure full population coverage. Data were gathered using a structured Likert-scale questionnaire adapted and analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, multicollinearity diagnostics, and multiple linear regression to empirically test the hypothesized relationships. Findings reveal that all three dimensions of audit quality positively and significantly influence fraud prevention, with audit evidence quality exerting the strongest effect, followed by auditor independence and competence. The study concludes that high-quality audits serve as a proactive mechanism for detecting irregularities, strengthening internal controls, and enhancing transparency in financial reporting. Based on these results, it is recommended that banks prioritize continuous professional development for auditors, enforce strict independence policies, and adopt robust systems to enhance audit evidence quality. Integrating these measures into governance frameworks will improve fraud prevention and safeguard financial integrity in Nigerian DMBs. Keywords: Audit Quality, Auditor Competence, Auditor Independence, Audit Evidence Quality, Fraud Prevention.

title: Cloud accounting readiness and strategic performance in Jordanian service companies and the moderating role of IT human capability
summary: This paper is based on the Resource-Based View (RBV) and the Dynamic Capabilities Theory. It focuses on understanding how cloud accounting readiness relates to strategic performance. In doing so, the paper aims to examine the moderating influence of Organizational IT Human Capability (OITHC) on the relationship between cloud accounting readiness and strategic performance of service companies in Jordan. Data were collected from 113 top managers. The study employs the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) statistical technique to analyze the impact of cloud accounting readiness on the strategic performance and assess the moderating effect of OITHC. The findings of the analysis indicate that cloud accounting readiness positively relates to the strategic performance. Furthermore, the effect of the cloud accounting readiness on strategic performance is positively moderated by OITHC. The results of the study show that organizations with advanced OITHC perform better in achieving superior strategic results with cloud accounting systems. This study expands the knowledge in the field by indicating that technological resources alone cannot lead to strategic benefits, while organizational capabilities are very important in this process. The study also highlights the indirect contribution of digital transformation to organizational sustainability by promoting resource efficiency, operational resilience, and long-term competitive performance.

title: Leakage-aware federated-style simulation for fraud risk prediction in AI-enabled FinTech platforms
summary: AI-enabled FinTech platforms increasingly rely on automated fraud-risk prediction to secure high-volume digital payments, mobile-money transactions, and real-time financial services. However, fraud detection remains difficult because fraudulent transactions are rare, financial data are sensitive, and centralized machine-learning models may create privacy and data-governance risks. This study evaluates a leakage-aware and imbalance-aware federated-style simulation for fraud-risk prediction in AI-enabled FinTech platforms. The study does not implement FedAvg, cryptographic secure aggregation, differential privacy, or model-parameter exchange. Instead, the PaySim Synthetic Financial Dataset was partitioned into five simulated FinTech clients, local models were trained separately, and prediction-level aggregation was used to compare centralized and simulated decentralized learning settings. The experimental workflow included data-quality assessment, leakage-aware feature selection, feature engineering, class-imbalance analysis, centralized model development, threshold optimization, and federated-style model comparison. The results show that fraud cases represented only 0.0466% of all transactions and occurred only in CASH_OUT and TRANSFER operations. The best-balanced centralized model was the Improved Random Forest at a threshold of 0.33, achieving an F1-score of 0.3019. Federated Ensemble Aggregation achieved the highest PR-AUC of 0.2699 and a precision of 1.0000, but its recall remained low at 0.1429. The centralized Improved Random Forest retained the highest F1-score of 0.3019, indicating a stronger overall precision-recall balance. Global feature-importance analysis showed that transaction amount, log-transformed amount, temporal features, transaction type, and destination-account activity were the main fraud-risk indicators. These findings should be interpreted as evidence from simulated decentralized fraud-risk learning rather than a full secure federated learning implementation.

title: Valorization of Biostimulant Made from Microalgae for Sustainable Tomato Production: Yield Enhancement and Carbon Mitigation Potency
summary: A sustainable biostimulant has been gaining more attention, as it provides eco-friendly agriculture practices and helps achieve sustainable results. This study investigated the effects of microalgae-based biostimulants on tomato seedling vigor, plant growth, and fruit productivity. Four microalgae biomasses from different strains and conditions were tested (Limnospira maxima in seawater and freshwater cultivation, Leptolyngbya sp. and Chlorella sp.) for the early stage of cultivation and later followed by testing in mature stages. Limnospira maxima freshwater was found to significantly improve germination up to 99.3% and reduced T50 from 38.4 to 29.6 h. It was also found to increase the mean germination time (MGT) from 12.6 to 9.96 h. Overall, the germination index (GI) increased from 1.2 to 1.6. Root length was also found to increase significantly in the microalgae biostimulant, similar to the effect of a commercial biostimulant. In terms of productivity, the algal-based biostimulant has higher fruit productivity than the control and commercial biostimulant (2.64 kg, 2.2 kg, and 1.9 kg, respectively). These findings highlight the potential of algal-based biostimulants for sustainable tomato crop cultivation for clean agriculture practices in semi-arid environments. Linking to the carbon footprint, the application also avoided emissions of more than 14,000 kg CO2 equivalent per hectare per crop cycle. These outcomes position locally produced microalgae biostimulants as a green product that couples crop productivity with carbon mitigation and supply chain resilience in semi-arid environments.

title: Digital transformation and organisational performance: The mediating role of marketing agility among guesthouse operators in Accra Metropolitan District
summary: This study examines how digital transformation influences organisational performance, with marketing agility as a mediating variable, among guesthouse operators in the Accra Metropolitan District, Ghana. A survey of 301 employees and managers from 51 guesthouses was conducted using questionnaires and partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was conducted in SmartPLS version 4.1.1.4 to analyse the research model and its associated hypotheses. The results show that digital transformation has a significant positive relationship with marketing agility. Marketing agility fully mediates the relationship between digital transformation and guesthouse performance. The study also found a significant positive relationship between marketing agility and guesthouse performance. However, the direct relationship between digital transformation and guesthouse performance was not statistically significant, indicating that digital transformation alone does not drive organisational performance. Instead, marketing agility is the key, an underexplored link that makes digital transformation effective. It is recommended that guesthouses adopt tailored digital tools, social media platforms and emerging technologies and develop flexible marketing strategies that adapt to changing customer needs to boost performance and remain competitive in the industry.

title: Digital Transformation of Insurance: Reconstructing Legal Certainty Through Critical Intercultural Communication in Indonesia’s Economic Law Framework
summary: Digital transformation has reshaped the insurance industry, yet research remains dominated by normative legal perspectives that treat legal certainty primarily as a regulatory matter. Consequently, how legal certainty is constructed and negotiated through communication within digital insurance ecosystems remains underexplored. This gap is particularly evident in Bandung and Pontianak, Indonesia, where regulatory fragmentation, intercultural complexities, and power asymmetries shape digital insurance practices. This study reconstructs legal certainty through Critical Intercultural Communication using Constructivist Grounded Theory (CGT). Thirty participants were selected through theoretical sampling: eight regulators and policymakers, eleven insurance and InsurTech professionals, and eleven digital insurance consumers. The analysis generated four categories: Communicating Legal Meaning in Digital Insurance, concerning the negotiation of legal meanings; Negotiating Intercultural Legitimacy and Public Trust, addressing legitimacy and trust across cultural and institutional positions; Constructing Communicative Digital Governance, examining communication, coordination, and accountability; and Reconstructing Legal Certainty through Communicative Power, explaining how power relations shape access to legal meaning and legitimacy. These categories informed the substantive Communicative Legal Certainty Reconstruction Model (CLCRM), conceptualizing legal certainty as an ongoing communicative process shaped by meaning, legitimacy, governance, and power. The study integrates Critical Intercultural Communication and Economic Law, advancing an understanding of legal certainty beyond formal norms toward communicative processes that sustain legitimacy, trust, and compliance. It offers theoretical foundations for more adaptive, inclusive, and equitable digital insurance governance.

title: Design and analysis of an intelligent audit risk assessment system based on retrieval-augmented large language model
summary: Audit risk assessment is increasingly challenged by complex financial environments and the limited ability of traditional data-driven models to capture contextual information. Existing approaches mainly depend on structured financial indicators and often overlook regulatory knowledge and narrative disclosures. This study proposes an intelligent audit risk assessment framework that integrates a retrieval-augmented large language model (RAG-LLM) with a Bayesian–logistic hybrid estimation mechanism. The framework integrates financial, governance, operational, and textual data with audit standards, regulatory cases, and historical accounting irregularities to support context-aware risk evaluation. The proposed system was evaluated using an economically calibrated synthetic dataset consisting of 612 firm-year observations across 14 industries from 2018 to 2024. Results show that the RAG–LLM Bayesian hybrid model achieves an out-of-sample AUC of 0.912, outperforming gradient boosting (0.754), random forest (0.723), and logistic regression (0.694). It also achieves improved calibration performance with a Brier score of 0.088 and a misclassification rate of 6.7%. Further analysis shows that LLM-derived reasoning constructs contribute 48.3% of the total explanatory contribution. The findings demonstrate that retrieval-enhanced reasoning improves prediction accuracy, interpretability, and decision support capability for intelligent auditing systems.

title: 32. MANAGERIAL PROFILE, ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE READINESS AND SUSTAINABLE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN SMES: A CONCEPTUAL REVIEW OF PERFORMANCE AND COMPETITIVENESS DRIVERS
summary: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are increasingly exposed to technological acceleration, competitive pressure, sustainability requirements and uncertainty. In this context, their performance and competitiveness depend not only on financial or technological resources, but also on the strategic profile of their managers. This article develops an integrative conceptual review of how the managerial profile shapes SME performance and competitiveness through artificial intelligence (AI) readiness and sustainable digital transformation. Drawing on Upper Echelons Theory, the Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capabilities Theory and the Technology-Organization-Environment framework, it argues that managers’ education, experience, digital openness, innovation orientation, risk-taking propensity and strategic vision influence the firm’s ability to prepare for AI, adopt digital technologies and integrate sustainability into organizational practices. The review connects previously fragmented streams of literature on managerial characteristics, AI readiness, digital transformation, sustainability orientation and SME competitiveness, and proposes a conceptual framework in which AI readiness and sustainable digital transformation mediate the relationship between the managerial profile and SME performance. The article contributes theoretically by positioning the managerial profile as a micro-foundation of SME transformation, conceptually by developing an integrative model, and managerially by emphasizing the importance of digital literacy, data-driven decision-making, responsible leadership and sustainability awareness. The framework is particularly relevant for Moroccan SMEs, which face challenges related to digital maturity, managerial capabilities, innovation, financing and institutional support.

title: Optimal multi-period dynamic portfolios for sustainable investing
summary: Sustainable investing involves balancing traditional investment strategies with environmental, social, and governance-related (ESG) objectives to improve long-term outcomes. We develop a stochastic control framework for constructing optimal multi-period dynamic ESG portfolios, in which investors form dynamic portfolios by maximizing utility functions that account for both profitability and the average ESG scores of their portfolios in the near and distant future. We provide an explicit solution to the investors' utility maximization problem, and show that the optimal weight is a linear combination of three components: a financial performance component, an ESG component, and a component reflecting the weight from the previous period. Using the U.S. stock market data, we find that the multi-period dynamic ESG portfolio outperforms single-period portfolios in terms of Sharpe ratios, alphas, and ESG scores. Our article extends the dynamic portfolio theory in the context of sustainable investing, and provides guidance to practitioners on tailoring ESG portfolios to their specific preferences and to market conditions related to ESG.

title: Sustainability-Driven Luxury Hotel Choice: The Role of Eco-Consciousness, Sustainable Values, and Fintech Adoption among Young Travellers in Sri Lanka
summary: This study explores how young travellers understand and interpret sustainability when selecting luxury hotels in Sri Lanka. Specifically, it investigates the meanings and experiences associated with eco-consciousness, perceptions toward eco-sustainability, and eco-sustainable values, while also examining how sustainability initiatives implemented by luxury hotels and fintech-enabled services are perceived within the hotel selection process. By addressing a gap in understanding the lived experiences and perspectives of young travellers, the study contributes to emerging discussions on sustainability-oriented luxury consumption within an emerging tourism destination. Guided by an interpretivist research philosophy and an inductive qualitative approach, the study collected primary data through semi-structured interviews with purposively selected young travellers and luxury hotel managers in Sri Lanka. The research was informed by the Theory of Reasoned Action as a sensitizing theoretical framework. Data were analysed using thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns, perceptions, and meanings associated with sustainable luxury hotel selection. The findings reveal that sustainability is increasingly viewed by young travelers as an integral component of luxury hospitality rather than an optional attribute. Participants associated eco-sustainable practices with authenticity, ethical responsibility, and enhanced travel experiences. Visible sustainability initiatives, environmental transparency, and community-oriented practices emerged as important considerations in hotel evaluations. Fintech-enabled services were perceived as facilitating sustainable travel experiences by improving convenience, transparency, and engagement with sustainability-related initiatives. However, participants also expressed concerns regarding the credibility and visibility of sustainability claims, highlighting the importance of trust and effective communication. This study is limited to the Sri Lankan luxury hotel sector and reflects the perspectives of a purposively selected group of participants. As a qualitative study, the findings provide contextual insights rather than statistical generalizations. Future studies may examine these themes across different tourism settings and cultural contexts. The study provides original qualitative insights into how young travelers make sense of sustainability within luxury hospitality settings. By bringing together sustainability, luxury tourism, and fintech-enabled services within a qualitative framework informed by the Theory of Reasoned Action, the study contributes to a deeper understanding of the beliefs, perceptions, and experiences underlying sustainable luxury hotel choice among younger generations in an emerging market context.

title: ORGANIZATIONAL AND ECONOMIC MODEL OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN THE REGIONAL LIGHT INDUSTRY: MECHANISMS AND FORECAST TO 2030 (EVIDENCE FROM BUKHARA REGION, UZBEKISTAN)
summary: The article proposes an organisational and economic model for managing the digital transformation of light industry enterprises as a driver of regional economic development. Based on an empirical assessment of 25 textile enterprises in the Bukhara region, which revealed a moderate and uneven level of digital maturity (mean Digital Transformation Index, RTI = 0.506), the model transforms digital transformation from a spontaneous process into a managed, phased, and measurable five-stage cycle comprising diagnostics, strategy, infrastructure, implementation, and monitoring. The model is differentiated according to digital maturity groups, with the validity of the grouping confirmed by analysis of variance (ANOVA; F = 79.76; p < 0.001). Three supporting mechanisms are substantiated: a regional digital competence centre, a multi-source financing system, and a digital export platform. A three-scenario forecast to 2030 indicates that, under the target scenario, the regional RTI will increase from 0.45 to 0.80, labour productivity will rise by 60%, and textile exports will grow by 77%, with an investment efficiency ratio of 10.08.

title: An Empirical Juridical-Digital Twin Integrating Blockchain Traceability, Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, and Demand-Signal Optimization for Micro-Enterprise Supply Chains in Pesisir Barat
summary: Background: Micro-enterprises operating along the Pesisir Barat coastline experience chronic product spoilage and demurrage because logistics are fragmented and contractual enforcement under the Indonesian Civil Code (KUHPerdata) is weak. Objectives: This study aims to construct a juridical-digital twin that (1) optimizes logistical performance through multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), (2) guarantees compliance with Articles 1320, 1338, and 1243 of the KUHPerdata, and (3) allocates risk transparently via blockchain-based smart contracts. Methods: A three-layer architecture was implemented. The physical layer collects high-frequency IoT data (GPS, temperature, wave height, fuel flow). The digital-twin layer simulates the supply-chain using a Markov decision process whose state vector S_t^i=[GPS_t,T_t,Hs_t,F_t,D_t] and action set A_t^i={route, temp}. Reward R_t^i= -alpha·Spoilage_t^i -beta·Demurrage_t^i -gamma·P_legal^i + δ·ServiceLevel_t^i incorporates a legally calibrated penalty P_legal derived from smart-contract clauses. Policy-gradient updates Delta θ=alpha∇_θ logπ_θ(A_t|S_t)(G_t-V_θ(S_t)) were trained on 12 months of pilot data. Demand forecasting employed a calibrated LSTM (24-h window, 128-unit hidden layer, MSE loss). Legal constraints were encoded as Solidity smart contracts: Clause 1 triggers liquidated-damage payments for temperature breaches; Clause 2 defines force-majeure based on BMKG wave-height advisories; Clause 3 enforces a good-faith risk-sharing rule limited to 10 % of contract value. title: Can rural e-commerce policies enhance the total factor productivity of agricultural enterprises? Causal inference based on dual machine learning models
summary: Introduction Rural e-commerce policies, as an important component of the digital economy, are profoundly reshaping the agricultural value chain and food supply chain, and are of great significance for enhancing the economic efficiency of the grain industry. Methods Based on the panel data of 231 A-share agricultural listed enterprises in China from 2010 to 2024, this paper takes the comprehensive demonstration policy of e-commerce entering rural areas in China as the standard natural experiment, constructs A dual machine learning model, and systematically examines the impact of rural e-commerce policies (RECP) on the total factor productivity (TFP) of agricultural enterprises and its mechanism of action. Results The research findings are as follows: (1) RECP significantly enhanced the TFP of agricultural enterprises. After introducing high-dimensional fixed effects, replacing machine learning algorithms, and using instrumental variable methods to alleviate potential endogeneity, the conclusion remained robust. (2) Mechanism analysis indicates that RECP mainly promotes the improvement of TFP in agricultural enterprises by reducing information asymmetry, increasing R&D investment and optimizing the human capital structure. (3) Heterogeneity analysis shows that this promoting effect is more significant in enterprises in the growth stage, those with lower financing constraints, those engaged in agricultural product processing, and large listed agricultural enterprises. Discussion The research conclusion provides new empirical evidence for understanding the micro-mechanism by which the digital economy empowers the productivity improvement of listed agricultural enterprises, and offers policy implications for enhancing the supporting digital ecosystem of listed agricultural enterprises.

title: Effect of Sustainability Disclosure on Financial Performance of Deposit Money Banks in Nigeria
summary: This paper looks at how sustainability disclosure affects the financial performance of deposit money banks (DMBs) in Nigeria. The paper checks the single effect of social sustainability reporting (SSR), environmental sustainability reporting (ESR), economic sustainability disclosure (ECSD), and corporate governance disclosure (CGD) on bank profit. The study uses 11 listed Nigerian deposit money banks from 2010 to 2025, giving 176 bank-year points of data. Disclosure was measured with Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) content analysis, while financial performance was measured with return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), net interest margin (NIM), and return on capital employed (ROCE). Firm size and leverage were used as control variables. The paper used pooled OLS, fixed effects (FE), and random effects (RE) panel regression, and the Hausman test was used to pick the best model for each equation. The Hausman test picked the fixed effects model in all four cases. The result shows that ESR has a good and significant effect on ROA, NIM, and ROCE. SSR has no significant effect on any of the four measures. ECSD has a bad and significant effect on all four measures. CGD also has no significant effect on any measure. Firm size pushes performance up in all models, while leverage pulls performance down. The paper says that regulators and bank managers should pay more attention to the quality of environmental disclosure, since this is the one type of disclosure that keeps helping bank profit in Nigeria.

title: Usage of blockchain technology and shareholder-oriented firm performance: Evidence from Indian listed firms
summary: Blockchain technology (BCT) is increasingly used to improve transparency and reduce information asymmetry within firms, yet evidence on how its usage affects shareholder-oriented firm performance (SFP) remains scarce, especially in emerging economies. This study examines whether usage of blockchain technology is associated with SFP among non-financial firms listed on the National Stock Exchange of India from 2016 to 2024. Usage is measured as a time varying binary indicator drawn from Compustat Global database and validated through textual analysis of annual reports. SFP is measured using the price to book value ratio, earnings per share, and the dividend payout ratio. A two-step system generalized method of moments estimator is used to address dynamic persistence and endogeneity, based on 3,501 firm year observations for 389 firms using BCT. The results show that usage of blockchain technology is positively associated with all the three measures. The association is significant at the 5 percent level for earnings per share and at the 10 percent level for the price to book value ratio and the dividend payout ratio. The study contributes to the fintech and corporate finance literature by providing multi-indicator evidence from an emerging market. It also offers implications for managers, investors, and policymakers who evaluate the financial returns to blockchain investment. The findings should be interpreted with caution given the modest significance levels and the binary measure of BCT usage.

title: Timing Differences in ESG Ratings’ Recognition of Quantity and Quality Signals in Green Patents
summary: Whether ESG rating agencies can distinguish the quantity from the quality of green patents, and whether the two are recognized at different points in time, remains an open question. This article decomposes green patents into applications (quantity), authorization (certification quality) and citations (market influence), and uses panel data of China’s A-share listed companies from 2010 to 2024 to examine the time series structure of its impact on ESG ratings. We find that the quantitative signal is immediate—patent applications significantly and consistently boost ESG ratings—while the qualitative signal is significantly lagging: patent citations are not positively related during the same period (the common sample estimate is significantly negative), and their impact only turns positive and reaches a peak in the second lag period, conveying significantly more information than the quantitative signal. This “quantity is immediate, quality-lagged” model still holds true under nonlinear settings and a series of robustness tests. The root cause is the delay in the inclusion of citation information by rating agencies. The results show that ESG ratings use the time dimension to distinguish quantitative expansion and quality improvement in green patents, which provides a possible information basis for identifying “greenwashing” behavior and improving rating information processing.

title: When politics meet accounting: the moderating effect of corporate political connections on the reporting quality-investment efficiency nexus in India
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine the association between financial reporting quality (FRQ) and firms’ investment efficiency and investigates whether corporate political connections moderate this relationship in India. Design/methodology/approach Using an unbalanced panel of 413 non-financial firms listed on the S&P BSE 500 index from 2010 to 2021, we construct three FRQ measures and a composite index and estimate fixed effects panel regressions. We address potential endogeneity using two-stage least squares with the leave-one-out industry-year-mean FRQ as an instrument. Robustness checks employ alternative investment efficiency specifications and bias correction procedures. Findings Higher FRQ is significantly associated with greater investment efficiency across all specifications. Single-party connections strengthen the positive association between FRQ and investment efficiency and its association with lower overinvestment, while the moderating effect of multi-party connections is statistically inconclusive. These findings are robust to endogeneity corrections and alternative specifications, though less robust for overinvestment under bias correction. Originality/value This study provides a theoretically grounded examination of how political connections heterogeneity shapes the governance role of FRQ. By distinguishing single-party from multi-party connections, the study contributes to the literature on political economy and accounting-based governance in emerging markets.

title: Exploring the Moderating Role of Innovation Capabilities in the ESG Disclosure–Firm Performance Relationship: Evidence From an Emerging Market
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines how innovation capabilities moderate the relationship between ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) disclosure and firm performance for Nifty 500 firms from 2015 to 2025. Firm performance is measured using ROE, ROA, and Tobin's Q, while innovation is captured through R&D intensity, technical know‐how (TKH), and patents, representing both tacit and codified forms of knowledge. The study employs fixed‐effects panel regression, with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, panel‐corrected standard errors (PCSE), and system GMM employed to ensure the reliability and robustness of the findings. The results show that ESG disclosure has a positive effect on profitability, operational efficiency, and market valuation. The sub‐components further reveal that Environmental (ENV), Social (SOC), and Governance (GOV) dimensions individually contribute to improved firm performance, although the magnitude of these effects varies across performance measures. R&D intensity and technical know‐how consistently strengthen the positive effects of ESG disclosure and its sub‐components ENV, SOC, and GOV dimensions, suggesting that firms with greater learning capacity and technological depth are better equipped to convert sustainability commitments into superior financial and market results. Patents exhibit mixed moderating effects, dampening accounting‐based performance while improving market valuation by signaling long‐term technological potential. Overall, the findings underscore innovation as a critical capability through which ESG disclosure translates into superior firm performance, suggesting that managers should integrate ESG initiatives with investments in innovation capabilities to maximize the performance benefits of ESG, while policymakers should strengthen ESG disclosure frameworks and promote innovation‐oriented policies to foster sustainable corporate growth in emerging markets.

title: Sector-wise ESG Risk Score Analysis of Indian Companies: A Comparative Study
summary: Responsible investment philosophies like Environmental, Social and Governance have emerged as a comprehensive response to different societal challenges. The ESG thinking provides a structured approach to align investment decisions with long-term sustainability and responsible development goals. Quantitative and descriptive research design is implemented for the secondary data of ESG data for the period of 2024. The data is initially analysed using summary statistics to understand the distribution pattern of the data, additionally ANOVA is used to study the significant difference in mean ESG scores across different sectors and the final results reveals that there is a statistically significant difference in mean ESG risk across various sectors.

title: ВПРОВАДЖЕННЯ ESG-ПІДХОДІВ У ДІЯЛЬНІСТЬ ПІДПРИЄМСТВ ІНДУСТРІЇ ТУРИЗМУ ТА ГОСТИННОСТІ
summary: Концепція ESG, що виникла як інструмент нефінансового оцінювання бізнесу на фондових ринках, за останнє десятиліття трансформувалася у ключовий елемент стратегічного управління підприємствами реального сектору економіки, зокрема туристичного та готельно-ресторанного бізнесу. У статті досліджено теоретичні та прикладні аспекти впровадження ESG-підходів (Environmental, Social, Governance) у діяльність підприємств індустрії туризму та гостинності України в умовах воєнного та післявоєнного відновлення економіки. Розкрито сутність ESG-концепції як інструменту забезпечення сталого розвитку туристичного та готельно-ресторанного бізнесу, систематизовано підходи вітчизняних і зарубіжних дослідників до оцінювання рівня ESG-трансформації в готельно-ресторанній, курортно-рекреаційній та туроператорській діяльності. На основі статистичних даних Державної служби статистики України, Державного агентства розвитку туризму України, Всесвітньої туристичної організації та галузевих досліджень за період 2011-2025 рр. побудовано динамічний ряд показників кількості суб’єктів індустрії туризму та гостинності та частки підприємств, які впроваджують елементи ESG-практик. Здійснено регресійний аналіз залежності рівня ESG-трансформації підприємств індустрії туризму та гостинності від часового фактора, за результатами якого отримано рівняння лінійного тренду з коефіцієнтом детермінації R² = 0,859, що свідчить про статистично значущу та стійку тенденцію до зростання показника. На основі побудованої регресійної моделі сформовано прогноз показника на 2026-2028 рр., згідно з яким частка підприємств індустрії туризму та гостинності з ESG-практиками може досягти майже 30 відсотків. Проаналізовано міжнародний досвід упровадження ESG-стандартів в індустрії туризму та гостинності (стандарти K-ESG, ESRS/CSRD, GRI), визначено ключові бар’єри та перспективні напрями ESG-трансформації українських підприємств індустрії туризму та гостинності в умовах післявоєнної відбудови та європейської інтеграції. Обґрунтовано практичні рекомендації щодо гармонізації вітчизняної галузевої практики нефінансової звітності з європейськими вимогами та поетапного впровадження галузевих стандартів ESG-оцінювання.

title: Auditing Creativity in Large Language Models: Value, Semantic Diversity, and Generation Budgets
summary: Assessments of language-model creativity can change when evaluation moves from distinct wording to distinct ideas, excludes low-value outputs, or accounts for how a system generates and selects candidates. This paper develops a mathematical audit of these changes, building on established distinctions among quality, novelty, and diversity. A distributional ledger separates reference-relative novelty, externally assessed value, semantic diversity conditional on value, and generation and selection budgets. Exact finite-distribution results characterize reward tilts, sequence and token temperature, likelihood-based judging, and filtering versus ranking. The entropy derivative retains a covariance with the base log-probability: alignment can diversify or concentrate outputs even while divergence from the base increases. Preservation and contrastive cancellation results identify their assumptions and the additional identification requirements needed for deployment. A reproducible secondary analysis examines 132,000 released NoveltyBench responses from six models, two generation conditions, and two prompt sets. The complete paired analysis retains 131,520 responses. At ten candidates and a quality-score threshold of seven, in-context generation increases the mean number of semantic groups whose first representative qualifies by 4.63 on curated prompts and 1.70 on WildChat, with paired prompt-bootstrap intervals of [4.15, 5.11] and [1.56, 1.84]. Qualification reduces the corresponding unfiltered coverage gains by approximately 28 percent and 37 percent. Some descriptive model rankings change, while positive coverage gains persist across thresholds and after excluding judge-model name overlaps. Released judgments, representative-only scoring, and unequal context costs limit interpretation; no new human validation, historical-originality measurement, or causal alignment claim is made. Controlled numerical checks verify the mathematical implementation, and a prospective protocol specifies the evidence still needed. The contribution is an intervention audit and an empirical demonstration of measurement sensitivity, rather than a new creativity taxonomy or a universal creativity score.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR DETECTING PUBLIC PROCUREMENT FRAUD THROUGH ESG RISK INDICATORS: A QUALITATIVE SECONDARY STUDY OF SDG 16
summary: Public procurement absorbs 12.7% of GDP across OECD countries (OECD, 2025), and bribery to win public contracts featured in 57% of concluded foreign-bribery cases in the OECD’s 2014 analysis. This study asks whether AI-enabled screening that incorporates environmental, social and governance (ESG) indicators can deliver accountable procurement-integrity gains, and under what conditions. It uses a qualitative, theory-informed secondary comparative design: three core cases (Brazil, Ukraine, Italy), two supplier-side illustrations (Odebrecht, Grenfell Tower) and two algorithmic-accountability comparators (the Netherlands, Australia), assessed against a five-level evidence hierarchy running from operational scale to verified outcomes. Governance and procedural indicators are operational; no reviewed case demonstrates validated environmental or social integration. Reported benefits mostly measure exposure, activity or self-reported savings; low selectivity, signal decay and weak follow-through limit effect; and automated enforcement without due process has caused severe harm elsewhere. The paper contributes the ESG-Integrity Analytics Framework (EIAF), five testable propositions and a replicable evidence-grading protocol, and concludes that AI’s contribution to SDG 16.5, 16.6 and 16.10 is conditional on validation, institutional follow-through and accountability.

title: TC-HGAT: A Task-Conditioned Hierarchical Graph Attention Network for ESG Text Classification
summary: Classifying corporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosures is challenging because they combine technical terminology with subtle, domain-specific distinctions. Pretrained Transformers such as ClimateBERT perform well but require many parameters and substantial GPU memory. This paper introduces TC-HGAT, a lightweight hierarchical graph attention network with task-semantic conditioning. TC-HGAT uses frozen FastText-300D embeddings and builds, for each document, a graph of word nodes, virtual cluster nodes, and a task-semantic node obtained by mean-pooling the embeddings of a natural-language task description. On three ESG tasks (Claim, Specificity, and Commitment), TC-HGAT achieves macro-F1 scores of 94.6%, 77.8%, and 79.3%, with the highest mean scores on Claim and Commitment, although no difference from ClimateBERT is statistically significant. Most of the gain comes from the task-semantic node, which improves macro-F1 significantly on all three tasks (by 5.7, 2.4, and 4.5 points), whereas the cluster layer alone gives a modest improvement that is significant only on Claim. Random vectors in the same graph position, including a norm-matched one, do not reproduce this gain, indicating that it depends on the content of the task representation. TC-HGAT trains about 1.4 million parameters, far fewer than BERT-base and ClimateBERT, and needs substantially less peak GPU memory during training.

title: Auditing First-Finisher Inference: A Reproducible Replay Study
summary: A first-finisher policy changes the composition of a model pool as well as its response time. We adapt an established all-subsets estimator to audit that change using complete correctness and timing records. A local study fits 96 random forests with deliberately mixed tree budgets and records 103,680 single-image inference calls. Across three overlapping digits-data splits, eight-candidate serial-time replay reduces accuracy by 9.97–11.16 percentage points relative to a uniformly selected candidate. An exploratory decomposition attributes almost all of this loss to budget composition. A full independent timing rerun preserves the eight-candidate loss, but changes a 32-candidate result by 5.28 points. The artifact provides an inspectable stress test and sensitivity analysis, not a new estimator, an LLM result, or a concurrent-serving speedup measurement. AI assistance. AI tools assisted literature discovery, manuscript drafting, code generation and checking, mathematical checks, and reproducibility analysis. The supplied project records do not identify exact tool/model versions for this paper. The reported classifier predictions and serial timings come from executed computations; the supplement identifies separate synthetic simulations. No LLM inference or physical concurrent-serving experiment was performed. Materials and attribution. The classifier study uses the scikit-learn digits subset of Alpaydin and Kaynak (1998), Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits, https://doi.org/10.24432/C50P49, CC BY 4.0. No digit images are included. The all-subsets estimator and concentration bound retain attribution to the cited prior work. The five-page supplement is included with the manuscript. Author-review and submission-approval notes in the PDFs were written during draft preparation. This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.
